tasks.task_intent: Audit or inspect sites for environmental performance and look into suspected breaches of the rules.
tasks.prompt: Invented case: residents report muddy water flowing from a housing construction site into a creek after storms. As the environmental specialist for the county, write the investigation plan: what you review before the visit (the site's stormwater permit and erosion control plan), what you inspect on site (silt fences, inlet protection, stabilized entrances, sediment basins), samples or photos you collect and how, interviews, how you determine whether a violation occurred, and the documentation for possible enforcement.

rubric.description: Reviews the permit, plan and past inspection history before visiting.
Collects defensible evidence (dated photos, sampling with chain of custody, field notes) tied to permit requirements.
Links observations to specific permit conditions and documents findings for enforcement.

reference_answer_outline: Review permit coverage, erosion and sediment control plan, inspection logs.
Inspect controls and discharge points; photograph with GPS and time.
Turbidity samples upstream and downstream with chain of custody.
Interview site superintendent; request maintenance records.
Findings report referencing permit conditions and required corrective actions.

tasks.task_intent: Log measurement data and produce reports, summaries and graphs explaining what the results mean.
tasks.prompt: Invented data: you sampled dissolved oxygen, temperature, pH, conductivity and E. coli at four creek sites monthly for a year. Write the data report for the watershed council: how data were recorded and quality-checked (calibration logs, duplicates, holding times), a summary table, two charts you would include (with types and axes), comparison with the state water quality criteria (cite the source type), and plain-language findings with limitations.

rubric.description: Describes recording, calibration and QC checks and how flagged data were handled.
Tables and charts are appropriate, labeled and compare sites and seasons.
Compares with applicable criteria correctly and states limitations and next steps.

reference_answer_outline: Field sheets, meter calibration records, field duplicates, E. coli holding time compliance.
Table of seasonal medians by site.
Charts: time series of dissolved oxygen by site; bar chart of E. coli geometric mean.
Criteria from the state water quality standards; exceedances noted.
Findings: downstream site lower oxygen in summer; recommend source investigation.

tasks.task_intent: Review submitted applications and supporting records to decide whether an applicant qualifies or is liable.
tasks.prompt: Invented case: a small furniture-finishing shop applies for a minor-source air permit, reporting that it uses 3,000 liters of solvent-based coatings a year. Write the review: the information you check for completeness, how you estimate emissions from coating usage and solvent content (show the calculation with labeled assumptions), whether the shop's estimate qualifies it for the requested permit type, missing records you would request, and the decision memo.

rubric.description: Checks required application elements and supporting records (safety data sheets, purchase records).
Emission estimate uses volume, density and VOC content correctly with stated assumptions.
Decision memo ties conclusions to rules and identifies deficiencies or conditions.

reference_answer_outline: Checklist: facility information, process description, materials, controls, signatures.
Emission estimate: liters times density times VOC fraction gives kilograms per year.
Compare with the permit threshold in the applicable rules.
Request safety data sheets and 12 months of purchase records.
Memo: approve with recordkeeping conditions or request more information.

tasks.task_intent: Monitor how development projects affect the environment.
tasks.prompt: A state highway widening will fill 0.8 hectares of wetland and cross a trout stream; the permit requires monitoring during construction and for five years afterward. Write the monitoring plan: indicators (turbidity, temperature, macroinvertebrates, wetland vegetation, hydrology at the mitigation site), locations and frequency, methods and quality control, thresholds that trigger corrective action, and annual reporting.

rubric.description: Indicators match the impacts and permit conditions.
Uses control and impact sites, before and after data, and appropriate frequency.
Defines thresholds and corrective actions and a reporting schedule.

reference_answer_outline: Before-after-control-impact design with upstream reference site.
Continuous turbidity and temperature during construction; macroinvertebrates spring and fall.
Mitigation wetland: vegetation cover, invasive species, groundwater levels.
Thresholds: turbidity over background triggers inspection and stopping work; low native cover triggers replanting.
Annual reports to the permitting agency.

tasks.task_intent: Talk customers through test results and what the analysis means.
tasks.prompt: Invented case: a family's private well test shows nitrate at a level above the federal drinking water standard for public systems and detects total coliform bacteria. The parents have a 3-month-old baby. Write the phone conversation script and follow-up letter: how you explain the results clearly without alarming or minimizing, immediate precautions (especially for infant formula), what the coliform result may mean, retesting and treatment options, and where they can get further help.

rubric.description: Explains results and standards correctly in plain language.
Prioritizes the infant's safety with correct precautions (do not boil water for nitrate; use an alternative source for formula).
Gives retesting, treatment options and referrals to health department or certified contractors.

reference_answer_outline: Result explanation with units and the standard as a comparison.
Nitrate: boiling concentrates it; use bottled water for formula and drinking now.
Coliform: indicator of possible contamination; shock chlorination and retest.
Treatment options for nitrate such as reverse osmosis or ion exchange; well inspection.
Letter with results, advice, contacts and retest date.

tasks.format: notice of violation and conversation plan
tasks.task_intent: Tell violators about their infractions and the penalties they face.
tasks.prompt: Continuing the construction runoff case, the inspection confirmed failed silt fences and sediment reaching the creek. Write the notice of violation letter and a plan for the conversation with the site manager: the facts and the permit conditions violated, required corrective actions with deadlines, potential penalties under the applicable rules (refer to the rule type without inventing amounts), the right to respond, and how you keep the tone firm but professional.

rubric.description: Notice cites dates, observations, evidence and exact permit conditions.
Corrective actions and deadlines are specific and verifiable.
Explains penalties and rights accurately, keeps a professional tone and documents the conversation.

reference_answer_outline: Heading, permit number, inspection date and observations with photo references.
Conditions violated, quoted by number from the permit.
Corrective actions: repair silt fence within 48 hours, stabilize slopes, clean creek sediment under guidance.
Penalty language referencing the enforcement rules; right to respond within a set period.
Conversation: firm facts, listen, agree on reinspection date, written follow-up.

tasks.task_intent: Talk with the client about the product, the ad concepts and approach, and what the copy should change.
tasks.prompt: You wrote three radio-spot scripts for a family-owned furniture store's spring sale, and the owner wants to 'make it louder and mention every brand'. Plan the client meeting and write the follow-up: questions to clarify goals and audience, how you explain why fewer messages work better in a 30-second spot, two revised directions you will propose, how you capture agreed changes and approvals, and the revised script for one direction.

rubric.description: Questions uncover goals, audience, offer details and legal requirements (sale terms).
Explains copy choices respectfully with reasons, offering options rather than refusing.
Agreed changes and approvals are documented, and the revised script fits 30 seconds.

reference_answer_outline: Questions: who buys, what single reason to come in, sale dates and exclusions.
Explain one big idea per spot and a memorable call to action; brand list on the website.
Options: a warm family-business story or a focused price-and-urgency spot.
Change log with approval sign-off and deadline.
Revised script of about 75 words with sale dates and a clear call to action.

tasks.task_intent: Answer information requests from journalists or assign the right spokesperson or source.
tasks.prompt: Invented case: a water main break has closed the main campus of a community college for the day, and three reporters are calling. As the PR specialist, write the media response protocol: how inquiries are logged, who is authorized to speak on which topics, a holding statement you can release within 30 minutes, key messages and facts to confirm, how you handle questions you cannot answer yet, and when and how you issue updates.

rubric.description: Holding statement is timely, factual and avoids speculation.
Authorizes the right people for each topic and routes reporters accordingly.
Defines an update schedule, channels and how corrections are handled.

reference_answer_outline: Inquiry log: outlet, reporter, deadline, question, response.
Spokespeople: college president for decisions, facilities director for technical details, PR for logistics.
Holding statement: what happened, safety, closure, where updates are posted.
Unknowns: say what is being checked and when more will be shared.
Updates at set times on the website and social channels; final statement on reopening.

tasks.task_intent: Write and present on-air news, sports or weather items, collecting source material and reworking it so listeners get the facts within the time slot.
tasks.prompt: Take a real recent press release from a local government or university (cite it) and rewrite it as (1) a 30-second radio news story and (2) a 15-second headline version. Follow broadcast style: short sentences, active voice, attribution first, numbers rounded and written for the ear, phonetic spelling of difficult names. Then note what you would verify or add by calling a source before air, and time your read.

rubric.description: Copy is conversational, active, uses attribution first and is written for listening.
Keeps the most important facts and does not distort the source.
Lists facts to confirm and shows that the read fits the time slots.

reference_answer_outline: Lead with the most important change for listeners.
Attribution before claims: 'City officials say...'.
Round numbers; avoid lists; phonetic guide for names.
Verify dates, numbers and quotes with the source office.
Timed read: about 75 words for 30 seconds, 35 to 40 for 15.

tasks.task_intent: Plan the structure of a writing project and organize the material to fit it.
tasks.prompt: You are writing a 2,500-word magazine feature on how a small town rebuilt its main street after a flood. You have 14 interview transcripts, city records, and photographs. Create the project plan and outline: the central angle, the structure (opening scene, nut graf, sections), where each source and quotation fits, what you still need, a fact-checking plan, and a writing schedule to deadline.

rubric.description: Clear angle, nut graf and section logic suited to a feature.
Maps sources and quotations to sections and identifies gaps.
Includes fact-checking and a realistic schedule.

reference_answer_outline: Angle: the rebuild as a story of choices and trade-offs, not just recovery.
Opening scene with a business owner on the morning after the flood.
Sections: the flood, the debate over rebuilding, money and rules, what changed, what remains.
Gaps: insurance figures, city engineer interview, before-and-after data.
Fact-check names, numbers and timeline; schedule draft, edit and revision dates.

tasks.task_intent: Build and keep cooperative relationships with community, consumer, employee and public-interest groups.
tasks.prompt: A regional hospital plans to expand its emergency department, which will mean two years of construction next to a residential neighborhood. Write a stakeholder relations plan: map stakeholder groups (neighbors, patient advocates, employees, local businesses, city officials), what each cares about, the channels and frequency for each, a community advisory group design, how feedback is tracked and answered, and how you will measure trust over time.

rubric.description: Identifies groups with their interests and influence and tailors engagement.
Emphasizes listening, response and follow-through, not just announcements.
Defines indicators such as complaint resolution time, survey trust scores and advisory group participation.

reference_answer_outline: Map: neighbors (noise, traffic, parking), patients (access during construction), employees (parking, safety).
Channels: monthly newsletter, construction hotline, text alerts, quarterly open house.
Advisory group with neighbors and advocates; published meeting notes.
Feedback tracker with response times.
Indicators: complaints resolved within a set time, semiannual survey, attendance.

tasks.task_intent: Research background information to get ready for programs and interviews.
tasks.prompt: You will host a 10-minute live radio interview with a real local official or researcher of your choice about a current issue. Prepare the research brief: the guest's background from reliable sources (cited), the issue's key facts and competing viewpoints, five open-ended questions in a logical order with follow-ups, one fact you checked twice, pronunciation notes, and how you would handle an evasive answer on air.

rubric.description: Uses credible, cited sources and presents the issue's viewpoints fairly.
Questions are open-ended, ordered logically and include follow-ups.
Includes verification, pronunciation and a respectful strategy for evasive answers.

reference_answer_outline: Guest profile with role, track record and relevant statements, cited.
Issue background with numbers and timeline.
Questions from context to tough accountability question with follow-ups.
Double-checked fact with two sources.
Evasion strategy: polite restatement, specific follow-up, note for listeners.

tasks.task_intent: Help build a scheme for classifying documents and content so information is easy to capture, search and retrieve.
tasks.prompt: A mid-sized city's planning department has 120,000 scanned and born-digital files (permits, site plans, council memos, public comments, inspection photos) sitting in shared drives with inconsistent folder names. Draft a classification taxonomy and metadata scheme for a new content-management system: top-level categories and two levels below, five to eight required metadata fields with controlled values, how retention and public-records status are captured, and how you would test the scheme with real staff searches.

rubric.description: Categories are mutually exclusive enough to file consistently and reflect how planning staff actually look things up (by parcel, project, document type).
Required fields use controlled vocabularies or formats (parcel ID pattern, dates), and public-records and retention status are captured.
Proposes testing with real tasks, such as staff filing samples or finding items, and measuring agreement or time to find.

reference_answer_outline: Top level by function (permits, plans, meetings, enforcement, public input), then project or parcel, then document type.
Required metadata: parcel ID, project number, document type, date, author unit, public-records flag, retention category.
Controlled lists for document type; validation pattern for parcel IDs.
Card-sort or tree-test with about ten staff; measure filing agreement and search success.
Plan for migrating legacy folders with automated suggestions plus manual review.

tasks.task_intent: Study the available information to decide whether to install a new system or change an existing one, then recommend and plan that work.
tasks.prompt: A regional food co-op tracks member volunteer hours in a spreadsheet shared by five coordinators; hours are lost, duplicate member records exist, and the board wants monthly reports. Gather what you would need to know and write a recommendation memo: current-state problems, three options (fix the spreadsheet with structure and validation, adopt an off-the-shelf volunteer tool, or build a small web app), a comparison on cost, effort, data quality and maintenance, your recommendation, and a rollout plan for the chosen option.

rubric.description: Problems are traced to causes (no unique member ID, free-text entry, concurrent editing) using evidence the student says they would collect.
Options are compared on consistent criteria including who maintains the solution after the student leaves.
The recommendation includes data cleanup, migration, training and a check that reports match after cutover.

reference_answer_outline: Interview coordinators and sample the sheet to count duplicates and gaps.
Option table: cost, setup time, data validation, reporting, maintenance burden, privacy.
Likely recommendation: an off-the-shelf tool or structured form plus database, since a custom build has no long-term maintainer.
Migration: deduplicate members on name plus email, import historical hours, reconcile totals.
Train coordinators; run the old and new systems in parallel for one month.

tasks.task_intent: Work with front-end and back-end developers so a website project is delivered completely.
tasks.prompt: You designed the new course-catalog website for a community college: search with filters, course detail pages, and a 'plan my semester' view. Two front-end developers and one back-end developer start building next week. Write the collaboration plan: what you hand off (components, states, responsive breakpoints, accessibility notes), which decisions you need from the back-end developer (search API fields, response times), how design questions get answered during the build, and how you review the built pages against the design.

rubric.description: Handoff covers interaction states (empty, loading, error), responsive behavior and accessibility, not just static mockups.
Identifies what design needs from the back end (data fields, filter values, pagination) and flags design choices that affect performance.
Defines a regular review routine with acceptance criteria for design fidelity and accessibility.

reference_answer_outline: Component inventory with states and tokens (colors, spacing, type) in a shared design file.
Breakpoints for phone, tablet and desktop; keyboard and screen-reader notes for filters.
Questions for back end: which fields are searchable, filter counts, latency target, handling of sections with no seats.
Twice-weekly design check-ins and a shared question log with owners.
Review each page against acceptance criteria, including WCAG contrast and focus order.

tasks.task_intent: Find out what document-management capabilities a department or its users actually need.
tasks.prompt: A hospital's research office wants a document-management system for study protocols, consent-form versions, and regulatory correspondence; three research teams currently use email attachments and personal drives. Write a needs-assessment plan and a sample findings summary: who you will talk to, the questions you will ask, which existing documents you will inventory, how you will capture compliance needs (version control, audit trail, retention), and a prioritized list of requirements written as clearly invented example findings.

rubric.description: Includes coordinators, investigators, regulatory staff, IT and records management, not only managers.
Combines interviews, a document inventory, and observation of a real workflow such as a consent-form amendment.
Findings are written as testable requirements and ranked by risk and frequency; example findings are labeled as invented.

reference_answer_outline: Stakeholder list and a 30-minute interview guide on current workflow, pain points and must-not-lose items.
Inventory of document types, volume, and where the authoritative version lives.
Compliance needs: version history, approval trail, controlled access, retention schedule.
Requirements such as: only the current approved consent version can be downloaded for enrollment.
Ranked by risk (regulatory findings) and frequency of use.

tasks.task_intent: Design, build and change software systems, relying on quantitative models and analysis to forecast how a design will behave.
tasks.prompt: A university wants a notification service that texts students when a seat opens in a full course section. Write a short design document: the components (enrollment feed, waitlist store, notifier, rate limiter), a simple queueing or load model that estimates peak messages per minute during registration week from stated assumptions, how that estimate drives design choices, and how you would measure in production whether the model was right.

rubric.description: Components and data flow are clear, including how duplicate or stale notifications are prevented.
The load estimate uses stated assumptions (students, sections, open-seat events per hour) and the arithmetic is shown and plausible.
Plans to compare predicted and observed load and adjust capacity or design if they diverge.

reference_answer_outline: Event-driven design: enrollment change triggers a check of the waitlist and queues notifications.
Assumptions such as 20,000 students and 3,000 full sections, with a peak of seat changes in the first hour; computes messages per minute.
Result drives queue size, SMS provider rate limit and batching.
Idempotency key per student and section to avoid duplicate texts; expiry if the seat is taken.
Dashboards on queue depth and send rate; compare with the model after the first registration day.

tasks.task_intent: Write and edit technical documents for digital interface designs, such as user guides, test protocols and reports.
tasks.prompt: Your team redesigned the online form residents use to request a bulky-trash pickup from the city. Write two short documents: (1) a one-page help guide for residents, written at about an eighth-grade reading level and available in plain language for translation, and (2) a usability-test protocol for five participants that names the tasks, what you will observe, success criteria and how findings will be reported to the development team.

rubric.description: The help guide matches the form's steps, uses plain language and short sentences, and covers common errors.
Tasks are realistic, success criteria are observable, and the protocol includes consent and a think-aloud script.
Explains how findings are ranked by severity and turned into specific fixes for developers.

reference_answer_outline: Guide: what items qualify, step-by-step with screenshots placeholders, what happens after submitting, how to change a request.
Readability check with a standard formula; avoid idioms to ease translation.
Test tasks: request pickup for a couch, change the date, find out why a mattress is rejected.
Measures: task completion, time, errors, and post-task ease rating.
Report: severity-ranked issues, each with evidence and a recommended change.

tasks.task_intent: Plan how a piece of software will be checked: which scenarios to exercise, which scripts or manual steps to run, and in what order.
tasks.prompt: A student-run campus food-ordering app is about to ship a 'split the bill' feature that lets up to six friends share one order, each paying by card or meal-plan credit. Write the test plan for this feature: scope and out-of-scope items, at least eight named test scenarios (include rounding of odd cents, one payer's card being declined, and a friend leaving the group mid-checkout), which scenarios you would automate versus run by hand, test data you need, and the exit criteria for release.

rubric.description: Scenarios cover the normal path, boundary values (1 and 6 payers, odd-cent totals) and failure paths (declined card, timeout, member leaving), not only happy paths.
The split between automated and manual tests is justified by repeatability, risk and cost, and the test data needed is stated concretely.
Exit criteria are measurable (e.g. zero open severity-1 defects, all payment-path tests passing) and say who signs off.

reference_answer_outline: Scope statement naming the split-bill flow, payment providers and meal-plan ledger; excludes unrelated menu features.
Scenario table with ID, preconditions, steps and expected result; includes the cent-rounding rule (who absorbs the leftover cent).
Automates calculation and API-level payment tests; keeps exploratory and multi-device UX checks manual.
Lists test accounts, sandbox cards that decline, and a meal-plan balance near zero.
Exit criteria with severity thresholds and a named approver.

tasks.task_intent: Teach staff safe computing habits and build a culture of security awareness so the organization's systems stay protected and run smoothly.
tasks.prompt: A 40-person food-bank nonprofit just had a volunteer coordinator's email account taken over through a fake 'shared document' link, and the attacker emailed donors asking for gift cards. Design a 30-minute security-awareness session for staff and regular volunteers: three learning objectives, the agenda minute by minute, one realistic hands-on exercise built from this incident (no real victim names), and how you will measure whether behavior changed 60 days later.

rubric.description: Content suits non-technical staff and volunteers, uses the real incident pattern, and avoids jargon or blame.
Objectives translate into specific behaviors (checking sender domains, reporting suspicious mail, using MFA) that the exercise actually practices.
The 60-day measure is concrete, such as a simulated phishing click rate or report rate compared with a baseline.

reference_answer_outline: Objectives: recognize credential-phishing cues, report quickly through one named channel, turn on MFA.
Agenda: 5 min story of the incident, 10 min cue spotting, 10 min hands-on inbox triage exercise, 5 min MFA setup check.
Exercise uses three sanitized sample emails, one legitimate and two malicious.
Follow-up: simulated phish at day 45 to 60, compare click and report rates with a pre-session baseline.
Notes privacy: individual results are not used for discipline.

tasks.task_intent: Change existing software to fix defects, keep it working on new platforms or interfaces, and make it faster.
tasks.prompt: Your registrar's office runs a five-year-old Python script that exports course enrollments to a CSV for the state reporting portal. Since enrollment doubled it takes 40 minutes and times out, it crashes on student names with accented characters, and the portal is moving from CSV upload to a JSON API next term. Write a change proposal: diagnose the likely causes of each problem, the code changes you would make, how you will prove the new version produces the same records as the old one, and a rollback plan.

rubric.description: Each symptom gets a plausible technical cause (e.g. row-by-row queries, wrong text encoding) and a way to confirm it, such as profiling or a failing test case.
Changes are scoped and safe: performance fix, UTF-8 handling, and an output layer that supports both CSV and the new API without rewriting everything.
Equivalence is proven with a record-level comparison on real-sized data, and rollback is concrete.

reference_answer_outline: Profile first; likely N+1 database queries or loading everything into memory; fix with batched queries or a single join.
Encoding crash: read and write explicitly as UTF-8; add test names with accents and non-Latin scripts.
Separate data extraction from output formatting so a JSON API client can be added beside the CSV writer.
Verification: run old and new on the same snapshot and diff record counts and field values.
Rollback: keep the old script deployable and switch back with one configuration flag.

tasks.task_intent: Check that changes to a system work correctly and do not break anything before they are released.
tasks.prompt: A web app used by 3,000 club members is replacing its password-hashing library (from an old salted SHA-1 scheme to bcrypt) and will rehash each password when that user next logs in. Before deployment, write the regression checklist you would run: what must still work, the specific edge cases for users who have not logged in since the change, the security checks, the performance check on the login endpoint, and the go/no-go rule.

rubric.description: Covers migration edge cases: old-hash users, users mid-reset, accounts with very long or Unicode passwords, and the first login after deploy.
Each item has a pass condition, such as login latency under a stated threshold or no plaintext passwords in logs.
A clear go/no-go rule with what happens if a check fails, including a rollback path that does not lock users out.

reference_answer_outline: Core regressions: login, logout, password reset, account creation, session expiry.
Migration cases: legacy-hash user logs in and is rehashed; reset link issued before deploy still works or fails safely.
Security: confirm the bcrypt cost factor, no hashes or passwords in logs, rate limiting still on.
Performance: measure p95 login latency before and after; bcrypt cost tuned to stay within target.
Go/no-go: all severity-1 checks pass; rollback keeps both hash verifiers so no user is locked out.

tasks.task_intent: Coordinate how a computer-security plan is put into place, working with the organization's own staff and with outside vendors.
tasks.prompt: A three-office dental practice has bought two things: multi-factor authentication for its practice-management software, and a managed endpoint-protection service from an outside vendor. You are the security analyst coordinating the rollout over four weeks without disrupting patient scheduling. Write the coordination plan: who does what (practice staff, office managers, the MFA vendor, the endpoint vendor), the week-by-week schedule, how you will communicate with front-desk staff, and the three biggest rollout risks with mitigations.

rubric.description: Responsibilities of internal staff and each vendor are explicit, including who approves changes and who provides support at each office.
Sequencing protects clinic operations: pilot first, after-hours installs, and no MFA enforcement on a full patient day without fallback.
Risks are specific (lost phones, legacy imaging PCs, vendor delays) and each has a workable mitigation.

reference_answer_outline: RACI-style table: analyst coordinates, office managers schedule staff, vendors install and support.
Week 1 pilot at one office; weeks 2 and 3 roll out to the others; week 4 enforce MFA and review.
Front desk gets a one-page guide and a named on-call contact during the first enforced day.
Risks: shared front-desk logins, old imaging workstations unsupported by the agent, phones unavailable; mitigations include hardware tokens and exceptions logged with an expiry date.
Success measures: percentage of accounts enrolled and endpoint agents reporting.

tasks.task_intent: Study what users need and what the software must do, then judge whether a design can be delivered within the available time and budget.
tasks.prompt: The university library asks for a study-room booking app: students reserve rooms from their phones, staff can block rooms for events, no-shows are released after 15 minutes, and it must work with campus single sign-on. You have two part-time student developers for eight weeks and no budget for paid services beyond existing campus hosting. Write a one-page feasibility memo: the requirements you would confirm with users, a rough effort estimate per feature, what fits in eight weeks, what you would cut or defer, and your recommendation.

rubric.description: Distinguishes must-have from nice-to-have requirements and names open questions to confirm with students and staff.
Effort estimates are broken down by feature, include testing and SSO integration risk, and add up within the stated capacity.
Recommends a specific scope (build, reduce, or buy/adapt existing tool) with the trade-offs stated.

reference_answer_outline: Must-haves: SSO login, view availability, book and cancel, staff block-out; nice-to-have: notifications, analytics.
Open questions: booking limits per student, accessibility needs, room check-in method for no-show release.
Estimate in developer-weeks per feature, with SSO and testing called out; total compared with about 16 part-time developer-weeks.
Defer push notifications and analytics; consider an existing open-source booking system if SSO support exists.
Recommendation with a scope, a timeline and the main risk.

tasks.task_intent: Set and consistently apply rules and routines that keep the classroom orderly.
tasks.prompt: You are starting the year with 24 second graders. Write your classroom management plan for the first two weeks: four or five positively stated expectations, the routines you will teach (arrival, transitions, bathroom, getting help, dismissal) and how each is modeled and practiced, how you recognize positive behavior, a calm and consistent response ladder for misbehavior, and how you partner with families. Note how you adjust for a student with ADHD and a student new to English.

rubric.description: Expectations are few, concrete, positively worded and suitable for seven-year-olds.
Each routine is explicitly modeled, practiced and reinforced during the first weeks.
Responses to misbehavior are calm, predictable and respectful, with individual supports for the two students.

reference_answer_outline: Expectations: safe bodies, kind words, listening ears, try your best, take care of our things.
Routines taught with model, practice, feedback; visual schedule.
Recognition: specific praise, class goal chart.
Response ladder: nonverbal cue, reminder, reset spot, conference, family contact.
Supports: movement breaks and checklists for the student with ADHD; picture cues and a buddy for the English learner.

tasks.task_intent: Watch and assess students' learning, behavior, social growth and physical well-being.
tasks.prompt: A third grader's reading progress has stalled, she seems tired in the mornings, and she has recently been alone at recess. Write an observation plan for the next three weeks: what you will observe and when (academic, behavioral, social, physical signs), the recording tools (running records, anecdotal notes, a simple frequency chart), how you keep notes objective, who you would consult (reading specialist, nurse, counselor, family), and when concerns would require a referral or a mandated report.

rubric.description: Covers academic, social, behavioral and health indicators at different times of day.
Tools and examples show objective, dated notes rather than judgments.
Involves the right specialists and family, and correctly states that suspected abuse or neglect must be reported under mandated-reporter rules.

reference_answer_outline: Running records twice a week; note fluency and errors.
Anecdotal notes at arrival, recess and after lunch; frequency of yawning or head down.
Objective phrasing: what was seen and heard, not interpretations.
Consult reading specialist and nurse; family conversation about sleep and well-being.
Referral to student support team if no progress; immediate report if signs of abuse or neglect.

tasks.task_intent: Get materials and the classroom ready for learning activities.
tasks.prompt: Plan the materials and room setup for a third-grade science morning with four rotating stations on how plants grow (seed dissection, measuring seedlings, light versus dark comparison, recording observations in journals). List every material per station with quantities for 24 students, the room layout, safety and cleanup considerations, labeled instructions students can follow without you, setup and reset timing, and a backup plan if seedlings did not sprout.

rubric.description: Materials and quantities are complete and fit group sizes.
Layout, instruction cards and timing let students rotate and work independently.
Includes safety (seed allergies, tools), cleanup and a realistic backup plan.

reference_answer_outline: Station lists: soaked bean seeds, hand lenses, rulers, plants in light and dark, journals.
Layout with traffic flow and a teacher check-in station.
Picture-based instruction cards; rotation timer every 12 minutes.
Safety: check allergies, no tasting, safe tools; cleanup kits.
Backup: photos of growth stages or fast-sprouting seeds started earlier.

tasks.task_intent: Adjust teaching approaches and materials to suit students' different needs and interests.
tasks.prompt: Your fourth-grade class is learning to compare fractions with unlike denominators. Assessment shows three groups: students who still struggle with what a fraction represents, students ready for the grade-level goal, and students who already compare fractions easily. Plan one 60-minute lesson with differentiation: the shared launch, three tiered tasks using manipulatives, number lines or real-world problems, how you move between groups, supports for a student with dyscalculia, and a common exit task.

rubric.description: Uses accurate representations (fraction strips, number lines, benchmark fractions, common denominators).
Tasks differ in support and complexity while all target the same concept.
Explains how groups are monitored and adjusted, with specific accommodations and a common exit task.

reference_answer_outline: Launch: which is more pizza, two-thirds or three-fifths?
Tier 1: fraction strips to build and compare; Tier 2: benchmarks and number lines; Tier 3: create and justify comparison problems.
Teacher rotates with guiding questions; flexible regrouping mid-lesson.
Dyscalculia supports: manipulatives, visual models, fewer problems, extra time.
Exit task: compare two fractions and explain using a model.

tasks.task_intent: Plan and run a balanced mix of teaching, demonstrations and hands-on time so students can observe, ask questions and investigate.
tasks.prompt: Plan a one-week first-grade unit on weather. Each day should balance short direct teaching, a demonstration, and work time in which children observe, ask questions and investigate (for example, a class weather chart, a cloud-in-a-jar demonstration, measuring rainfall). Write the daily plan with times, the guiding question for the week, how children record observations at their level, how you capture and use their questions, and how you assess learning once the week is over.

rubric.description: Each day includes brief instruction, a demonstration and substantial student investigation.
Children's questions are collected and used, and observations are recorded in age-appropriate ways (drawings, symbols, tallies).
End-of-week assessment checks understanding through talk, drawings or a simple performance task.

reference_answer_outline: Guiding question: how does the weather change, and how can we tell?
Daily routine: weather chart with symbols, 10-minute mini-lesson, 15-minute investigation.
Demonstrations: cloud in a jar, wind direction with a streamer, thermometer reading.
Question board that the class returns to each day.
Assessment: draw and tell about today's weather; class graph of the week.

tasks.task_intent: Teach students both one-on-one and in groups using methods such as explanation, discussion and demonstration.
tasks.prompt: Design a week of guided reading for a second-grade class with five reading groups and two students needing one-on-one support. Write the plan: how groups are formed from assessment data, the focus skill and text level for two of the groups, the structure of a 20-minute guided reading session, what the rest of the class does independently, how you deliver the one-on-one sessions, and how you track progress and regroup.

rubric.description: Groups are formed from specific assessment data and are flexible.
Session structure includes before, during and after reading with explicit teaching of a skill.
Independent work is meaningful and manageable, and progress tracking leads to regrouping.

reference_answer_outline: Groups from running records and phonics screening; regroup every few weeks.
Example: group A decoding long vowels at an early level; group C fluency and retell at grade level.
Session: book introduction, word work, supported reading, discussion, quick check.
Independent: literacy stations with clear routines and accountability.
One-on-one: daily 10-minute sessions with targeted phonics; progress chart.

tasks.task_intent: Work out loads, slopes, flows and stresses in materials so the design requirements can be fixed.
tasks.prompt: A park needs a 6 m long timber footbridge, 1.5 m wide, carrying a pedestrian live load of 4 kPa plus its own dead load. Prepare a calculation package for the two main beams: load takedown, maximum bending moment and shear, required section modulus for a stated allowable bending stress, deflection check against span/360, and a short note on what a full design would also check (lateral stability, connections, durability, local code requirements). Show units throughout.

rubric.description: Tributary width, load combination and moment and shear for a simply supported beam are calculated correctly.
Section is sized from the section modulus and checked for deflection with a stated modulus of elasticity.
Identifies the remaining checks and that the design must follow the governing code and be reviewed by a licensed engineer.

reference_answer_outline: Each beam carries half the deck: live load 4 kPa times 0.75 m plus dead load estimate.
Uniform load w; moment w L squared over 8; shear w L over 2.
Required section modulus equals moment over allowable stress; select a glulam or sawn size.
Deflection 5 w L to the fourth over 384 E I compared with 6000/360 mm.
Other checks: bearing, connections, lateral torsional buckling, vibration, preservative treatment.

tasks.task_intent: Share data, maps and other information at public meetings or hearings about construction projects.
tasks.prompt: The city proposes converting a four-lane arterial into two travel lanes, a center turn lane and bike lanes (a 'road diet'). Neighbors are worried about traffic backing up. Prepare a 10-minute presentation outline for the public hearing: the problem the project addresses with crash and volume data (use clearly invented example figures), maps or diagrams you will show, expected effects on travel time, how you will answer the three most likely objections, and how public comments will be recorded and answered.

rubric.description: Presents crash, speed and volume data in understandable visuals with honest labeling of estimates.
Anticipates objections (congestion, emergency access, business deliveries) with evidence-based answers.
Explains next steps and how comments influence the decision.

reference_answer_outline: Slides: existing cross-section and proposed cross-section diagrams, corridor map with crash locations.
Data: daily volume within the range where road diets usually work, crash history by type.
Expected travel-time change at peak hours from a traffic model, with uncertainty.
Answers on emergency vehicles using the center lane, loading zones, and a monitoring period.
Comment cards and an online form; responses published before the council vote.

tasks.task_intent: Produce technical reports and articles about developing water supplies or cutting water waste.
tasks.prompt: A small town water utility produces 2.0 million liters per day but bills customers for only 1.5 million. Write a technical report (executive summary and four sections, about two pages) on the water loss: a water balance using the standard categories of real and apparent losses, likely sources in this system (with invented but plausible figures), the field and data work needed to confirm them, the costs and savings of three reduction options, and a recommended plan.

rubric.description: Breaks non-revenue water into real losses (leaks, main breaks) and apparent losses (meter error, unbilled use) with consistent numbers.
Specifies how losses will be confirmed (district metering, acoustic leak detection, meter testing).
Options have costs, savings and payback, and the recommendation follows from them; the summary is understandable to the town council.

reference_answer_outline: Non-revenue water 0.5 million liters per day, 25 percent of production.
Split estimate: leakage, customer meter under-registration, unbilled authorized use such as flushing.
Field work: night flow analysis, acoustic survey, testing a sample of old meters.
Options: leak detection and repair, meter replacement, pressure management; cost and payback each.
Recommendation and a monitoring indicator for annual reporting.

tasks.task_intent: Visit project sites to track progress and confirm the work matches the design and meets safety and sanitation requirements.
tasks.prompt: You are the owner's field engineer on a two-story school addition, and tomorrow the contractor pours the second-floor concrete slab. Create the pre-pour and during-pour inspection checklist: items to verify against drawings and specifications (rebar size, spacing, cover, embedded items), concrete delivery and testing checks, site safety items, what you photograph and record, and what you do if you find nonconforming work an hour before the pour.

rubric.description: Items reference the design documents and include measurable checks (bar size and spacing, cover, slab thickness, mix ticket).
Includes fall protection, shoring and formwork checks, and field testing of concrete (slump, temperature, cylinders).
Defines a clear authority and procedure for stopping or delaying the pour and documenting the issue.

reference_answer_outline: Rebar per drawings, chairs for cover, laps, openings and embedded conduits in place.
Formwork and shoring inspected; edge protection; access routes.
Delivery tickets: mix design, time since batching, water added; slump and air tests; cylinders made per specification.
Daily report with photos, weather, crew counts.
If nonconforming: notify the contractor and engineer of record, issue a written notice, re-inspect before pour proceeds.

tasks.task_intent: Review development plans to estimate how they will affect traffic.
tasks.prompt: A developer submits plans for a 220-unit apartment complex with one driveway onto a two-lane collector road near an elementary school. Write the city's traffic impact review memo: estimate weekday peak-hour trips using a stated trip-generation rate (cite the source type you would use and label invented rates), distribute trips to the network, identify intersections and pedestrian routes to check, list conditions of approval you might require, and note what you would ask the developer's consultant to revise.

rubric.description: Uses a stated rate per unit for AM and PM peaks, shows the arithmetic, and distributes trips reasonably.
Considers school pedestrian routes, sight distance at the driveway and turn-lane needs.
Proposes specific, justified conditions or study revisions rather than general concerns.

reference_answer_outline: Rate assumption such as about half a trip per unit in each peak hour, giving roughly 110 peak trips.
Distribution by direction based on the street network and destinations.
Check the driveway, two adjacent intersections and the school crossing.
Conditions: left-turn lane if warranted, sidewalk connection, crosswalk improvements, sight-triangle clearance.
Ask for counts taken when school is in session and a queuing analysis.

tasks.task_intent: Create plans for new water supplies or for programs that make water use more efficient.
tasks.prompt: A growing town of 30,000 people expects summer demand to exceed its well capacity within six years. Develop a water efficiency program plan as an alternative or complement to drilling a new well: baseline demand by sector (invented but labeled figures), four efficiency measures (for example, irrigation scheduling, fixture rebates, tiered pricing, leak repair), estimated savings and cost per unit of water saved for each, an implementation timeline, and how you would measure actual savings.

rubric.description: States baseline demand by sector and a savings target linked to the capacity gap.
Each measure has estimated savings and cost per unit saved so they can be compared with the cost of a new well.
Savings are measured against weather-normalized baseline data, not assumed.

reference_answer_outline: Baseline: residential indoor, outdoor irrigation peak, commercial, and losses.
Measures: smart irrigation controllers, rebates for high-efficiency fixtures, seasonal tiered rates, leak repair program.
Cost per cubic meter saved for each versus the new well's cost.
Phased timeline over three years with outreach.
Monthly billing data compared with a weather-normalized baseline; annual report to council.

tasks.task_intent: Plan how a piece of software will be checked: which scenarios to exercise, which scripts or manual steps to run, and in what order.
tasks.prompt: Your team is releasing new firmware for a battery-powered soil-moisture sensor that reports over LoRa every 15 minutes and must last two years on two AA cells. Write a test plan for the firmware release: the test scenarios (normal reporting, weak radio signal, battery near cutoff, sensor disconnected, clock drift), which tests run on a simulator versus on real devices in a test rack, how you will measure power draw, and the release criteria.

rubric.description: Scenarios reflect embedded realities: power states, radio retries, brown-out, sensor faults, and long-duration behavior.
Explains what can be simulated versus what needs physical devices and instruments, and why.
Release criteria include numbers (average current in microamps, packet success rate, no watchdog resets over a soak period).

reference_answer_outline: Scenario list with expected behavior, including retry and back-off on weak signal and safe shutdown at low voltage.
Simulator for logic and timing; a rack of real sensors with programmable power supplies for power and radio tests.
Power measured with a current analyzer across sleep and transmit cycles; projected battery life computed.
72-hour soak test with fault injection.
Release only if projected battery life is at least two years and no resets occur.

tasks.task_intent: Check that computer hardware and attached devices meet their specifications by running tests and recording and analyzing the results.
tasks.prompt: You received the first ten prototype boards of a USB-C docking station meant to deliver 65 W to a laptop, drive two 4K displays and stay below 45 C on its case. Write a verification plan and a mock results summary: the tests you would run for each specification, the instruments needed, how many boards and repetitions, a results table (use clearly invented example numbers), and how you decide whether a failing spec is a design flaw or a board defect.

rubric.description: Every stated specification has at least one test with method and instrument (electronic load, thermal camera, display test patterns).
Sample size, repetitions and recording format are stated; example numbers are labeled as invented.
Distinguishes a systematic failure across boards from a one-board defect and states the next diagnostic step.

reference_answer_outline: Power delivery: step the load to 65 W and check voltage regulation and USB PD negotiation.
Display: dual 4K at 60 Hz with pattern tests and cable variations.
Thermal: case temperature at full load in a 25 C room after one hour, measured with a thermocouple and thermal camera.
Results table across all ten boards with pass or fail and spread.
Failure on most boards suggests a design issue (layout, component rating); a failure on a single board points to assembly; confirm by swapping parts.

tasks.task_intent: Change existing software to fix defects, keep it working on new platforms or interfaces, and make it faster.
tasks.prompt: A lab's data-acquisition program talks to an analog-to-digital converter through a driver written for an older microcontroller. The board is being redesigned around a newer chip with a different SPI peripheral and DMA support, and users also report that samples are occasionally dropped above 10 kHz. Write a plan to port and improve the driver: what you would isolate behind a hardware-abstraction layer, how DMA could fix the dropped samples, the tests that prove timing and data integrity, and what you would keep unchanged.

rubric.description: Identifies which code is chip-specific (registers, clocks, interrupts) and proposes a clean abstraction so application code is untouched.
Explains the dropped-sample cause plausibly (interrupt latency, buffer overrun) and how DMA with double buffering addresses it.
Tests include known input signals, sample counting, and timing measurement with a logic analyzer or oscilloscope.

reference_answer_outline: Define an ADC interface (init, start, read buffer) and move register-level code into a chip-specific module.
Use DMA with ping-pong buffers so the CPU handles full buffers instead of every sample.
Feed a known sine or ramp signal and check for gaps and correct sample count over long runs.
Measure SPI clock and chip-select timing with a logic analyzer against the converter's datasheet.
Keep the file format and user interface unchanged so lab users see no difference.

tasks.task_intent: Check that changes to a system work correctly and do not break anything before they are released.
tasks.prompt: A smart-thermostat company is pushing an over-the-air update that changes the heating control algorithm and the Wi-Fi reconnect logic. Before the update goes to 50,000 homes, write the checklist of tests and rollout gates: functional checks of heating and cooling, behavior when Wi-Fi drops mid-update, rollback if the update fails to boot, a staged rollout plan, and the telemetry signals that would stop the rollout.

rubric.description: Tests target the two changed areas plus the update mechanism itself, including power or network loss during installation.
Uses a staged rollout (internal devices, small percentage, larger percentage) with explicit gates between stages.
Names measurable telemetry thresholds (boot failures, reconnect failures, temperature-overshoot reports) that halt the rollout.

reference_answer_outline: Bench tests of the control loop with simulated temperature profiles; check overshoot and cycling.
Interrupt Wi-Fi and power at several points during update; the device must boot the previous image.
A/B firmware slots with automatic rollback on failed health check.
Stages: employees, 1 percent, 10 percent, everyone, with 48-hour observation each.
Halt if boot failure exceeds a small set rate or reconnect failures rise above baseline.

tasks.task_intent: Decide what the power supply must provide and how it is arranged, based on how the system must perform and on its design specifications.
tasks.prompt: You are designing the power system for a single-board computer used in a museum kiosk: a quad-core processor, 4 GB of RAM, a 10-inch touchscreen, Wi-Fi, and two USB ports that visitors may use to charge phones. Produce a power budget and supply specification: list each load with typical and peak current per voltage rail, choose the input supply rating with margin, decide which rails need switching regulators versus linear regulators, and explain how you protect the board if a visitor plugs in a faulty device.

rubric.description: All loads are listed per rail with typical and peak values from plausible datasheet-style figures, and totals are computed correctly.
Input rating includes margin, and regulator choices are justified by efficiency, heat and noise.
Includes current limiting or electronic fuses on USB ports, reverse-polarity and overvoltage protection.

reference_answer_outline: Rails such as 5 V for USB and display, 3.3 V for I/O and Wi-Fi, and around 1 V for the processor core.
Peak budget includes simultaneous USB charging at the port limit; supply sized about 25 to 30 percent above peak.
Buck converters for high-current rails; low-dropout regulator for the noise-sensitive radio or analog parts.
Per-port current-limit switches with fault flag; TVS diode and fuse on input.
Thermal check on regulators at peak load inside the kiosk enclosure.

tasks.task_intent: Set the performance standards a system has to meet.
tasks.prompt: A city transit agency is commissioning onboard software that shows next-stop announcements and real-time arrival predictions on bus screens, using GPS and a cellular link. Write the performance requirements section of the specification: latency from GPS fix to on-screen update, prediction accuracy, behavior during cellular outages, startup time, and resource limits on the onboard computer. For each requirement give a number, how it will be measured, and why that value matters to riders.

rubric.description: Each requirement has a specific value and unit rather than vague words like 'fast'.
Each has a test method (logged timestamps, field trials on set routes, induced outages).
Values are justified by rider experience or safety, such as announcing a stop before the bus reaches it.

reference_answer_outline: Stop announcement at least a set number of seconds before arrival at typical speeds.
Screen update within about 2 seconds of a GPS fix; prediction error within a stated band for most trips.
During outages, fall back to schedule-based predictions and label them; resume within a stated time after reconnect.
Boot to usable display within a stated time after ignition.
CPU and memory ceilings leave headroom on the onboard computer; measured during field trials on named routes.

tasks.task_intent: Design electronic parts, devices and systems for uses ranging from business and industry to medicine, defense and science.
tasks.prompt: A greenhouse cooperative wants a low-cost, battery-powered light sensor node that measures photosynthetically active light from near darkness to full sun and reports hourly by Bluetooth to a phone. Write a design proposal: block diagram, choice of sensor and why, the analog front-end or digital interface with its range and resolution, power budget and expected battery life, enclosure and environmental concerns (humidity, heat), and how you would calibrate and test it.

rubric.description: Block diagram and component choices fit the requirements (range, resolution, low power, wireless).
Includes numbers for measurement range, resolution, current draw and battery life with the arithmetic shown.
Describes calibration against a reference meter and environmental testing.

reference_answer_outline: Blocks: light sensor, microcontroller with Bluetooth Low Energy, battery and regulator, enclosure with diffuser.
Sensor choice: photodiode with filter or a digital light sensor; dynamic range covered with auto-ranging.
Power: sleep current in microamps, brief wake every hour; battery life estimate in months or years.
Enclosure: sealed, UV-stable, condensation control, cosine-corrected diffuser.
Calibrate against a reference quantum sensor at several light levels; humidity and temperature cycling.

tasks.task_intent: Meet clients, fellow engineers and other parties to discuss engineering projects and products, existing or planned.
tasks.prompt: A dairy farm owner wants a rooftop solar array with battery storage so the milking equipment and milk cooling keep running during grid outages, which happen several times each winter. Prepare for and write up the requirements meeting: the questions you will ask (loads, outage duration, budget, utility rules, future expansion), a simple load table you will fill in together, how you will explain the trade-off between battery size and outage coverage in plain language, and the written summary of agreed requirements and open items.

rubric.description: Covers critical loads, motor starting currents, outage length, utility interconnection rules, budget and site constraints.
Explains battery capacity, power rating and outage coverage in terms the owner can use to decide.
Ends with a summary of requirements, assumptions, open questions and next steps.

reference_answer_outline: Load inventory: vacuum pump, milk cooling compressor, water heater, lights; running and starting power.
Outage history and acceptable outage coverage target.
Plain explanation: power rating sets what can run at once; storage capacity sets for how long.
Utility interconnection and net-metering rules; roof structural check.
Summary memo with critical-load list, target backup hours, budget range and follow-ups.

tasks.task_intent: Keep one's knowledge and skills current as computer technology changes quickly.
tasks.prompt: Your hardware team must decide within a year whether to move future embedded products from an Arm-based microcontroller family to a RISC-V-based family. Write a technology-scan brief and a personal learning plan: summarize the current state of both ecosystems in your own words with cited sources (vendor documentation, standards bodies, technical articles), list what you need to learn to evaluate them fairly (toolchains, debug support, security features, supply), and a three-month plan of courses, evaluation boards and small experiments with how you will share findings with the team.

rubric.description: Uses verifiable, recent sources and distinguishes vendor claims from independent evidence.
Learning targets connect to the actual product decision (tools, ecosystem maturity, cost, long-term availability).
The plan has specific activities, deliverables and a way to share results with colleagues.

reference_answer_outline: Brief: instruction set licensing, available parts, toolchain and debugger support, real-time operating system support.
Criteria: power, performance per dollar, security features, supplier longevity, team skills.
Plan: month 1 reading and an online course; month 2 port a small firmware module to a RISC-V board; month 3 benchmark and write up.
Share via a lunch-and-learn and a written comparison table.
Note uncertainty and what would change the recommendation.

tasks.task_intent: Inspect electronic equipment and systems to confirm they meet specifications, safety standards and applicable codes.
tasks.prompt: Your company buys 500 external 48 V power supplies from a new vendor for a medical cart product. Write the incoming inspection procedure: the sampling plan, visual and marking checks (safety certification marks, ratings label), electrical tests (output voltage regulation, ripple, efficiency, leakage current, dielectric withstand on a sample), the records you keep, and what happens with a lot that fails. Explain why medical use raises the bar compared with office equipment.

rubric.description: Tests match the specification and safety standards for medical electrical equipment (e.g. leakage current limits) with the right instruments.
Uses a stated sampling plan with accept and reject numbers and records serials, results and instrument calibration.
Defines quarantine, supplier notification and disposition steps for a failed lot.

reference_answer_outline: Sampling per a standard acceptance plan; destructive dielectric testing only on a small sample.
Markings: certification to the relevant medical safety standard, ratings, polarity, country of origin.
Electrical: regulation from no load to full load, ripple with a bandwidth-limited oscilloscope, earth and touch leakage current.
Records with instrument IDs and calibration dates.
Failed lot: quarantine tag, supplier corrective action request, disposition by quality engineer.

tasks.task_intent: Coordinate installation, testing, maintenance or documentation work so it complies with specifications, codes and customer requirements.
tasks.prompt: A parking garage will install 20 Level 2 electric-vehicle chargers on a new 400 A service, with load management so the chargers share capacity. You are the electrical engineer coordinating the electrical contractor, the charger vendor, the utility and the building inspector. Write the coordination plan: the sequence from submittals to energization, the inspections and tests required, how you verify the installation meets the drawings and the electrical code, how load management is commissioned, and the documents handed over to the owner.

rubric.description: Steps from submittal review through rough-in, inspection, utility energization and commissioning are in the right order with dependencies.
Identifies key verification points (conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, ground-fault protection, labeling) and required inspections.
Includes functional testing of load management under realistic loads and a complete turnover package.

reference_answer_outline: Submittals: charger data sheets, panel schedules, single-line diagram; engineer review.
Rough-in inspection, then final inspection by the authority having jurisdiction.
Tests: insulation resistance, torque checks, ground-fault protection operation, phase rotation.
Load management commissioning with several vehicles or test loads to confirm current sharing and limits.
Turnover: as-built drawings, test reports, warranty, network configuration and training.

tasks.task_intent: Study what users need and recommend suitable computer hardware.
tasks.prompt: A college media department is replacing 24 workstations used for 4K video editing, color grading and some 3D animation, with a budget of about $3,000 per seat. Interview notes (invented) say renders take too long, the shared storage is slow, and two editors are color-blind-friendly-display advocates. Write the recommendation: how you translated user needs into hardware requirements (CPU, GPU, memory, storage, displays, network), two configurations compared, the benchmark or test you would run before buying, and the final recommendation within budget.

rubric.description: Each hardware choice is traced to a user need or workload characteristic.
Two configurations are compared fairly, with a realistic pilot benchmark using the department's actual projects.
Stays within budget and addresses the network and shared-storage bottleneck, not only the desktop.

reference_answer_outline: Workload: GPU-accelerated editing and grading, CPU threads for rendering, 32 to 64 GB memory, fast local scratch storage.
Displays: color-accurate panels with calibration hardware.
Bottleneck: 10-gigabit network to the shared storage or local cache workflow.
Pilot: render and playback tests on two loaner configurations with real department projects.
Recommendation with per-seat cost and the network upgrade cost.

tasks.task_intent: Lead and coordinate the engineers and technicians who design, build, modify or test aircraft and aerospace products.
tasks.prompt: You are the junior engineer leading a five-person team (two design engineers, a composites technician, a test technician and an instrumentation intern) through a static load test of a new carbon-fiber wing spar for a small uncrewed aircraft. The test must show the spar carries 1.5 times the limit load without failure. Write the coordination plan for the three-week campaign: who does what, the sequence from specimen fabrication to test report, the safety controls for loading to failure, the instrumentation plan, and how you handle a schedule slip if the first specimen has a manufacturing flaw.

rubric.description: Each person's responsibilities and handoffs are explicit, and the sequence (fabricate, inspect, instrument, test, analyze, report) is logical.
Instrumentation (strain gauges, load cells, deflection) and load steps are appropriate for verifying the 1.5 factor, with predicted values to compare against.
Includes test-area exclusion zones and stop criteria, and a realistic fallback for a flawed specimen.

reference_answer_outline: Week 1: fabricate two specimens, ultrasonic or visual inspection, strain gauge placement plan.
Week 2: test-rig checkout, calibration of load cell, dry run at low load, test-readiness review.
Week 3: incremental loading to limit load, then to 1.5 times, holding and recording; optional test to failure.
Safety: shields, exclusion zone, abort criteria on unexpected strain or cracking sounds.
Contingency: second specimen built in parallel; report delays communicated with a revised date.

tasks.task_intent: Read and make sense of blueprints, technical drawings, schematics and computer-generated reports.
tasks.prompt: Use a publicly available mechanical drawing of a machined bracket or shaft (or sketch an invented one with at least one hole pattern, a tolerance block, a surface-finish note and two geometric tolerances such as position and flatness). Write a review memo for the machine shop: explain in plain words what each critical dimension and geometric tolerance requires, identify the datum features and how the part would be fixtured for inspection, flag any ambiguity or missing information, and list questions you would ask the designer before release.

rubric.description: Geometric tolerances, datums, tolerance block and surface-finish notes are interpreted correctly.
Links requirements to how the part is made and inspected (fixturing on datums, measurement method).
Identifies real gaps or conflicts in the drawing and turns them into specific questions.

reference_answer_outline: Datum A primary face, B and C as hole or edge features; part located on these for inspection.
Position tolerance on the hole pattern relative to A, B, C explained as a tolerance zone; flatness on the mounting face.
Default tolerances from the title block apply to unlabeled dimensions.
Ambiguities such as missing material spec, unclear thread callout or conflicting dimensions.
Questions for the designer and a recommendation to fix before release.

tasks.task_intent: Investigate why parts fail or vary and find the underlying cause.
tasks.prompt: Invented case: warranty data show a compact car's rear wheel bearings failing at about 30,000 km in one region, three times the normal rate, starting with vehicles built after a supplier change in March. Write a root-cause analysis using a structured method (such as 8D, fishbone and five whys): the problem statement, containment actions, the candidate causes across material, process, design and usage, the data and teardown tests you would request to confirm or rule out each, and how you will verify the permanent fix.

rubric.description: Uses a recognized method with a clear problem statement (what, where, when, how many) and containment.
Candidate causes are specific and each has a test or data check to confirm or eliminate it, rather than jumping to conclusions.
The permanent fix is verified with tests or field data and the process is changed to prevent recurrence.

reference_answer_outline: Problem statement with build dates, region, mileage and failure rate.
Containment: inspect stock from the new supplier, quarantine suspect lots.
Causes: seal design letting in road salt (region), heat treatment change at the supplier, press-fit tolerance at assembly.
Checks: teardown of failed parts for corrosion versus fatigue, hardness tests, compare press-fit force logs.
Verify fix with accelerated life testing and monitor warranty claims for six months.

tasks.task_intent: Build mathematical or computer models to create, assess or change a design so it meets the customer's engineering requirements.
tasks.prompt: A customer needs a quadcopter arm made of an aluminum tube that is 250 mm long, carries a 1.2 kg motor thrust at the tip, and must deflect less than 3 mm with a safety factor of 2 on yield. Build a simple analytical model (cantilever beam) to size the tube's outer diameter and wall thickness, show the equations and numbers, compare two candidate tube sizes, then explain how you would check the hand calculation with finite-element analysis and what extra effects (vibration, fatigue, joint stiffness) the simple model misses.

rubric.description: Uses correct cantilever bending stress and deflection relations with consistent units and a stated material property.
Compares candidates against both requirements and chooses one with mass considered.
Explains how FEA or testing would validate the model and names the missing effects with their likely impact.

reference_answer_outline: Load about 11.8 N; moment at root is load times 0.25 m.
Stress from bending moment times outer radius divided by second moment of area; deflection from load times length cubed over 3 E I.
Two tube sizes tabulated with stress, safety factor, deflection and mass.
FEA with matching boundary conditions; mesh check; compare with hand result within a few percent.
Missing effects: motor vibration and resonance, fatigue at the clamp, clamp compliance.

tasks.task_intent: Work with engineers and other staff to put operating procedures in place, solve system malfunctions or give technical information.
tasks.prompt: Invented case: a hospital's chilled-water system keeps tripping one of two chillers on low refrigerant pressure during hot afternoons, and the operating rooms are drifting above their temperature limit. You are the mechanical engineer meeting the facilities supervisor and the chiller service technician. Write a meeting script and follow-up note: what information you ask for (trend logs, alarm history, condenser water temperatures), likely causes you will discuss, the interim operating procedure to protect the operating rooms, and the agreed next steps.

rubric.description: Asks for specific data and observations that would distinguish likely causes rather than guessing.
Discusses plausible causes (fouled condenser, low charge, failing expansion valve, cooling tower performance) correctly.
Defines a safe interim procedure for critical spaces and clear next steps with owners and dates.

reference_answer_outline: Request: alarm times, suction and discharge pressures, condenser water supply temperature, recent service history.
Likely causes include a refrigerant leak, a faulty expansion valve or poor heat rejection on hot days.
Interim procedure: stage the healthy chiller first, pre-cool operating rooms in the morning, portable cooling backup.
Next steps: leak test, condenser tube inspection, cooling tower check; owners and dates.
Follow-up note circulated the same day with decisions recorded.

tasks.task_intent: Turn early vehicle design ideas into engineering requirements and estimates of what they will cost.
tasks.prompt: Your team is considering replacing a stamped-steel battery-tray bracket in an electric vehicle with a die-cast aluminum version to save mass. Write a short engineering specification for the new bracket (loads, crash and vibration requirements, corrosion protection, mass target, interface dimensions) and a rough per-unit cost estimate for both designs at 100,000 vehicles per year, including material, processing, tooling amortization and joining. State your assumptions and recommend whether to proceed.

rubric.description: Requirements are quantified and verifiable (load values, test standards, mass limit, interface tolerances).
The estimate separates material, process, tooling amortization and assembly with stated assumptions and correct arithmetic.
Weighs mass savings against cost, galvanic corrosion and supply risk and gives a clear decision.

reference_answer_outline: Specification: static and crash loads, vibration profile, salt-spray requirement, mass under a target, bolt pattern tolerances.
Steel: low material cost, cheap stamping, welding cost; aluminum: higher material cost, die-casting tooling amortized over volume.
Assumptions for prices per kilogram, cycle times and tooling cost.
Cost per kilogram of mass saved compared with the program's target.
Recommendation with risks such as dissimilar-metal joints.

tasks.task_intent: Set and consistently apply rules and routines that keep a classroom orderly.
tasks.prompt: You teach 10th-grade English with daily independent reading, small-group literature circles and a writing workshop with peer feedback. Write the classroom routines and expectations plan: the start-of-class routine, expectations for literature circle roles and discussion, how peer feedback stays kind and specific, phone and device expectations, what happens when expectations are not met, and how you teach the routines in the first two weeks.

rubric.description: Routines directly support reading, discussion and writing workshop rather than generic rules.
Expectations for discussion and peer feedback are concrete (sentence stems, role cards, feedback protocol).
Responses to unmet expectations are graduated, respectful and consistently applied.

reference_answer_outline: Start: 10 minutes of silent independent reading while attendance is taken.
Literature circle roles rotated; discussion norms posted.
Peer feedback protocol: one strength, one question, one suggestion, tied to the rubric.
Devices in a pocket chart unless used for drafting.
Responses: reminder, conference, adjusted seating, family contact; routines modeled with a fishbowl discussion.

tasks.task_intent: Fix or note any missing material, mistakes and inconsistencies found in copy.
tasks.prompt: Proofread this invented 120-word press release excerpt and produce an error log: "Riverside Community College are proud to announce it's new nursing lab, which open on Sept. 3rd, 2026. The lab, funded by a $1.2M grant from the Hartwell foundation, include 12 simulation beds, and a debriefing room. 'Our students deserve the best,' said Dean Maria Lopez. Dr. Lopez, who joined Riverside in 2019 will lead a ribbon-cutting on September 5. Tours are offered 10am-2pm and registration is required, visit riverside.edu/nursinglab." For each issue, record the location, the error type (grammar, punctuation, consistency, fact to verify), your correction, and whether it needs an author query.

rubric.description: Finds the subject-verb agreement, its/it's, date inconsistency (Sept. 3 versus September 5 and opening versus ribbon-cutting), missing commas and run-on sentence.
Corrections follow a consistent style and change no more than necessary.
Flags items that need confirmation (names, title Dean versus Dr., date logic, grant amount) instead of guessing.

reference_answer_outline: 'are' to 'is'; 'it's' to 'its'; 'open' to 'opens'; 'include' to 'includes'.
Remove serial-style comma before 'and a debriefing room'; add comma after 2019.
Style consistency for dates and times (September 3; 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.).
Fix the run-on: registration is required; visit the site.
Queries: Hartwell Foundation capitalization, the dean's title, whether opening and ribbon-cutting dates are correct.

tasks.task_intent: Teach a subject through explanation, discussion and demonstration.
tasks.prompt: Plan a 50-minute 11th-grade lesson on a short poem of your choice that is in the public domain (for example, by Emily Dickinson or Langston Hughes, if public-domain status is confirmed). Include a brief explanation of one literary concept (such as tone shift or extended metaphor), a teacher think-aloud demonstrating close reading of two lines, a structured small-group discussion, and a short written response. Explain how students move from your model to independent analysis.
