rubric.description: The concept is explained accurately and the think-aloud models evidence-based interpretation.
The lesson moves from modeling to guided practice to independent work.
The written task requires a claim supported by textual evidence and analysis.

reference_answer_outline: Concept mini-lesson with a simple definition and example.
Think-aloud on two lines: notice word choice, ask questions, form a claim.
Groups annotate the rest of the poem using a guiding question.
Share-out with evidence; teacher pushes for analysis beyond summary.
Exit paragraph: claim, quotation, explanation of effect.

tasks.task_intent: Check information or figures in one record against the same data elsewhere or against the original copy to catch mistakes.
tasks.prompt: A nonprofit's annual report has a typeset table of program results that must match the finance office's spreadsheet and the program staff's original text. Describe your verification procedure: how you compare figures (reading aloud with a partner, column totals, cross-footing), how you check names and titles against an authoritative list, what you do when the typeset text and the source disagree, and how you record and return corrections. Then create a short invented example with three discrepancies and show how each is logged.

rubric.description: Uses reliable comparison methods (partner reading, totals, cross-checks) covering every figure.
Does not silently choose a value when sources conflict; queries the author or source owner.
Each discrepancy is logged with location, both values, action and resolution.

reference_answer_outline: Two-person read-back of each figure; recompute totals and percentages.
Names and titles checked against the staff directory and donor database.
Conflicts sent as queries to the finance or program owner with both versions.
Corrections marked on the proof and logged in a tracker.
Examples: transposed digits, a total that does not add up, a misspelled donor name.

tasks.task_intent: Write, administer and mark tests and assignments that show how students are progressing.
tasks.prompt: Design the summative assessment for a four-week 9th-grade unit on argument writing: the prompt (with a choice of two debatable topics and a short source set), the analytic rubric with four criteria and performance levels, accommodations for students with IEPs and English learners, how you will grade consistently across 120 essays (anchor papers, calibration), and how students receive feedback they can use in the next unit.

rubric.description: The prompt and rubric measure the unit's goals (claim, evidence, reasoning, counterargument, conventions).
Includes anchor papers, calibration and accommodations that keep the same standard.
Feedback is specific, timely and connected to a next-step goal.

reference_answer_outline: Prompt with two topics and three short sources of varied perspectives.
Rubric criteria: claim, evidence, reasoning and counterargument, organization and conventions; four levels.
Accommodations: extended time, read-aloud of sources, bilingual glossary.
Grade with anchor papers; second-read a sample of essays.
Feedback: two strengths and one goal per student; a revision conference.

tasks.task_intent: Use standard proofreading symbols on copy to flag and fix typographic, layout, grammatical, punctuation and spelling mistakes.
tasks.prompt: Using standard proofreaders' marks (as in a major style manual), mark up this invented proof line by line and explain each mark: (1) "teh committee will meet on monday"; (2) "The results were suprising , and the team celebrated."; (3) a heading set in bold that should be italic; (4) a paragraph that should start on a new line; (5) two words that should be transposed: "the final report draft first". Provide both the margin mark and the in-text mark for each and note any house-style decisions you assumed.

rubric.description: Uses the standard marks for transposition, capitalization, deletion, spacing, new paragraph and font change.
Every error is marked in text and in the margin as conventions require.
Notes assumed house-style choices and stays consistent.

reference_answer_outline: Transpose mark for 'teh'; triple underline for capital M in Monday.
Insert letter in 'surprising'; close-up mark to remove the space before the comma.
Circle and 'ital' in margin for the heading; note bold removal.
New paragraph mark before the sentence.
Transpose 'report draft'; state that the style manual's marks were used.

tasks.task_intent: Keep a thorough written log of all lab work activities.
tasks.prompt: You are a technician running a PCR assay to screen 24 mosquito samples for a virus. During the run the thermocycler showed a lid-temperature error, you repeated two samples, and the positive control came up weaker than usual. Write the lab notebook entries for the day as you would in a regulated lab: header information, reagents with lot numbers and expiry, the plate map, the protocol and any deviations, the instrument error and what you did about it, results, and how corrections are made in the record.

rubric.description: Entries let another technician repeat the work: reagents, lots, volumes, equipment IDs, plate map, cycling conditions.
The instrument error, repeats and weak control are recorded factually with actions taken and their impact on results.
Entries are dated and signed, corrections are single-line strike-throughs or tracked edits with reason, and nothing is left for later memory.

reference_answer_outline: Header: date, project, technician, sample IDs and chain of custody.
Reagent table with lot numbers and expiry; master mix calculation.
Plate map with positive, negative and no-template controls.
Deviation: lid error at a stated cycle; repeated affected wells; noted weak positive control and decision on validity.
Results summary with interpretation criteria; supervisor review signature.

tasks.task_intent: Set and consistently apply rules and routines that keep a classroom orderly.
tasks.prompt: You are starting as a high school biology teacher with five sections of 28 students, and the first lab is a microscope and live-specimen activity in week two. Write your classroom routines and lab-safety rules plan: the five rules you will teach, entry and exit routines, how materials are handed out and collected, what happens when a rule is broken (with escalating steps), and how you will teach and practice the routines in the first week rather than just posting them.

rubric.description: Rules are few, specific and stated as expected behaviors, including lab safety items (goggles, handling glass slides, hand washing).
Routines for entry, materials and cleanup fit the lab space and time and reduce idle time.
Consequences escalate fairly and consistently, and routines are modeled and rehearsed, not only announced.

reference_answer_outline: Rules: follow lab instructions the first time, protect your eyes and hands, handle glassware and specimens as shown, keep your station clean, respect others' work.
Entry: warm-up question on the board; materials pickup by table captains.
Cleanup timer five minutes before the bell; checklist per station.
Consequences: reminder, private conversation, temporary removal from hands-on work with an alternative assignment, contact home.
Week-one rehearsal: practice runs, a safety quiz, and a signed safety contract.

tasks.task_intent: Stay current with clinical research practice and issues through reading the literature, continuing education and professional meetings.
tasks.prompt: You coordinate studies at a university clinical research office and the team asks you to keep them current. Prepare a one-page monthly current-awareness brief: choose two recent items you can actually find (for example, a regulatory guidance update on informed consent or decentralized trials, and a published paper on participant retention), summarize each in your own words, explain what changes for your studies, and list the sources you monitor regularly with how often you check them. Also describe how you would document continuing-education hours.

rubric.description: Items come from verifiable sources (regulator websites, peer-reviewed journals, professional associations) and are cited.
Each summary ends with concrete implications for the team's current studies or procedures.
Describes a realistic monitoring routine and continuing-education tracking, such as for coordinator certification.

reference_answer_outline: Two cited items with dates and links, summarized in plain language.
Implications such as updating consent templates or retention procedures.
Monitoring list: regulator guidance pages, ethics board newsletters, two or three journals, a professional coordinator association.
Monthly cadence; brief circulated by email and discussed at the team meeting.
Continuing-education log with date, topic, provider and hours.

tasks.task_intent: Oversee laboratory work to make sure it meets required standards.
tasks.prompt: Your biosafety level 2 teaching-and-research lab is preparing for an internal biosafety inspection in a month, and a recent near miss involved a student pipetting a bacterial culture outside the biosafety cabinet. Create a monthly self-inspection checklist and corrective-action procedure: items covering engineering controls, personal protective equipment, waste, training records and practices; the pass condition for each item; and how findings are assigned, fixed and verified.

rubric.description: Checklist items reflect real BSL-2 expectations (cabinet certification, signage, sharps and biohazard waste, eye wash checks, training records).
Each item has an observable pass condition, not vague wording.
Findings get an owner, due date and verification, and the near miss leads to retraining and a root-cause review.

reference_answer_outline: Cabinet certified within the last 12 months; airflow indicator working.
Biohazard signage with agent and contact; door closed during work.
PPE available and used; no open-toed shoes; gloves removed before leaving.
Waste: sharps containers below the fill line, autoclave logs complete.
Training records current for all users; corrective-action log reviewed by the lab manager.

tasks.task_intent: Teach a subject through explanation, discussion and demonstration.
tasks.prompt: Plan a 50-minute lesson for 10th-grade biology on natural selection. Include a short teacher explanation, a hands-on demonstration or simulation (for example, a predator-prey 'bead' or 'paper moth' activity), a structured discussion with three questions that push students past the misconception that individuals change because they need to, and a two-question exit ticket. Note how you would support English learners and a student with a visual impairment.

rubric.description: Explains variation, inheritance, selection and change in populations over generations correctly and targets a known misconception.
The demonstration produces data students use in discussion; timing is realistic for 50 minutes.
Includes specific supports for English learners and the visually impaired student and an exit ticket that tests understanding, not recall.

reference_answer_outline: Hook question and 8-minute explanation using a real example such as beak size in finches.
Simulation: colored beads on patterned fabric, three rounds of 'predation', students record surviving colors.
Discussion questions: did any bead change color; why did the population change; what would happen if the background changed.
Supports: word wall with visuals, sentence frames, tactile beads of different textures, partner roles.
Exit ticket: explain a population change scenario in two sentences.

tasks.task_intent: Carry out the procedures a study protocol requires at participant visits, such as interviews, vital signs and electrocardiograms.
tasks.prompt: Invented protocol: a blood-pressure medication trial requires, at week 4, a structured symptom interview, seated blood pressure taken three times after five minutes of rest, a 12-lead ECG, and a pill count. Write the visit procedure you would follow as the coordinator: preparation before the participant arrives, the step-by-step visit order, exact measurement conditions, what you do if a reading exceeds a safety threshold in the protocol, and how each item is recorded in the source documents.

rubric.description: Follows the stated conditions exactly (rest time, cuff size, three readings, order of procedures) and checks the visit window.
Defines the response to out-of-range readings or reported adverse events, including notifying the investigator promptly.
Records values, times, equipment IDs, deviations and the coordinator's signature in source documents before entry into the study database.

reference_answer_outline: Before: confirm visit window, consent version, calibrated equipment, ECG electrodes, case report form.
Order: interview first, then rest and blood pressure, then ECG, then pill count and return of unused study drug.
Correct cuff size, arm supported at heart level, no talking, readings one minute apart.
If above the protocol threshold, repeat, notify the investigator the same day, and document as a possible adverse event.
Source notes signed and dated; deviations reported per the sponsor's process.

tasks.task_intent: Analyze and process large datasets with statistical software.
tasks.prompt: Download a large public dataset such as a city's bike-share trip records for one year (millions of rows). Write an analysis plan and short report: how you load and process data that may not fit in memory, cleaning rules (zero-length trips, station errors, outliers), three questions you answer (for example, how ridership depends on weather and time of day), the methods and visualizations used, and the limitations. Include the main code steps in pseudocode or a language of your choice and cite the data source.

rubric.description: Uses chunking, databases or columnar formats appropriately and states hardware assumptions.
Cleaning rules are explicit and methods fit the questions (aggregation, regression with weather data).
Visuals are clear and limitations (missing data, station changes, causality) are stated.

reference_answer_outline: Read monthly files into a columnar format; aggregate with a query engine.
Rules: drop trips under one minute or over 24 hours, fix station ID changes.
Questions: hourly and weekday patterns, rain and temperature effects, busiest station pairs.
Methods: grouped summaries, regression of daily trips on weather, heatmaps.
Limitations: docked bikes only, membership changes, weather station distance.

tasks.task_intent: Set and consistently apply rules and routines that keep a classroom orderly.
tasks.prompt: You will teach algebra to four sections of ninth graders using frequent group problem-solving at vertical whiteboards. Write the norms and routines plan: expectations for group work (everyone contributes, mistakes are shared), how groups are formed and roles rotated, routines for starting a task, asking for help and sharing solutions, how you handle off-task behavior or one student doing all the work, and how you introduce the norms in the first week.

rubric.description: Norms support productive struggle and respectful critique of reasoning.
Grouping, roles, help-seeking and sharing routines are specific and practiced.
Responses to off-task or unequal participation are consistent and preserve students' dignity.

reference_answer_outline: Norms: explain your thinking, ask before telling, mistakes help us learn, one marker passes around.
Visibly random groups of three each day; roles rotate.
Help routine: ask group first, then signal the teacher with a question.
Unequal participation: assign the marker to the quietest student; check in privately.
First week: practice norms with low-stakes puzzles; reflect at end of class.

tasks.task_intent: Watch how a database performs and carry out the maintenance, upgrades or repairs it needs.
tasks.prompt: A genomics lab runs a PostgreSQL database of 400 million variant records that researchers query through a web portal; queries have slowed and the database version reaches end of support next year. Write a monitoring and maintenance plan: the performance metrics you track (query latency, slow-query logs, index usage, disk, cache hit rate), alert thresholds, routine maintenance (vacuum, statistics, backups with restore tests), how you diagnose a slow query, and the upgrade plan with testing and rollback.

rubric.description: Metrics and thresholds reflect database health and user experience.
Routine tasks and backup restore testing are appropriate for the database engine.
Upgrade plan includes a test environment, compatibility checks, a maintenance window and rollback.

reference_answer_outline: Track p95 query time, slow-query log, connections, disk growth, replication lag.
Alerts with thresholds and an on-call contact.
Maintenance: autovacuum tuning, analyze statistics, weekly full backup and monthly restore test.
Diagnose with query plans; add or adjust indexes; partition large tables by chromosome.
Upgrade: clone to test server, run portal test suite, schedule window, keep old cluster for rollback.

tasks.task_intent: Use feature-selection methods on models that predict outcomes such as sales, customer loss or health-care use.
tasks.prompt: A subscription meal-kit company gives you a dataset of 50,000 customers with 120 candidate features (order history, delivery issues, discounts used, survey answers) and asks for a model to predict cancellation in the next 60 days. Write the feature-selection plan: how you split data to avoid leakage (including features recorded after cancellation), at least two selection methods compared (for example, L1-regularized logistic regression and permutation importance from a tree model), how you evaluate the final model, and how you explain the selected features to the business team.

rubric.description: Uses time-based splits and removes features that would not be known at prediction time.
Compares at least two methods correctly, with cross-validation and stability checks.
Reports appropriate metrics (AUC, precision at a contact budget) and explains features without implying causation.

reference_answer_outline: Train on older customers, validate on later months; prediction date fixed for each customer.
Drop leaked fields such as cancellation survey answers.
L1 logistic path versus permutation importance in gradient boosting; keep features stable across folds.
Evaluate AUC and precision among the top 10 percent flagged.
Explain with plain charts; note correlations are not causes; propose retention test.

tasks.task_intent: Teach a subject through explanation, discussion and demonstration.
tasks.prompt: Plan a 50-minute Algebra 2 lesson introducing exponential growth. Include a demonstration (for example, folding paper or a simulated viral-sharing activity), a short explanation contrasting linear and exponential patterns in tables, graphs and equations, a discussion of a real context such as compound interest, and a formative check. Explain how you address the misconception that exponential growth is just fast linear growth.

rubric.description: Correctly distinguishes constant differences from constant ratios across representations.
Demonstration generates data students analyze.
Directly confronts the misconception and checks understanding with a task that requires distinguishing the two.

reference_answer_outline: Hook: would you take a fixed daily amount or a penny doubled daily for 30 days?
Demo: paper folding thickness table.
Compare tables: add versus multiply; graphs and equations.
Discuss compound interest with real rates.
Check: classify four tables as linear or exponential and justify.

tasks.task_intent: Record every change, modification and problem in a database.
tasks.prompt: In the genomics database from your earlier task, you added an index, changed a column type, and fixed a bug that had mislabeled 2,300 variant records for three weeks. Write the documentation: a change-log template and filled entries for the two changes, an incident report for the mislabeling bug (timeline, cause, affected data, users notified, fix, prevention), and the rules your team will follow so every future change is documented before it reaches production.

rubric.description: Entries include date, author, reason, exact change, testing done, approval and rollback steps.
Report covers timeline, root cause, scope of affected data, notification and prevention.
Defines a lightweight but enforced process (version-controlled migrations, review before production).

reference_answer_outline: Change log fields and two filled examples.
Incident timeline from introduction to detection to fix.
Affected records listed by query; researchers who downloaded them notified.
Prevention: automated test for label mapping, peer review.
Process: migrations in version control, ticket required, release notes posted to users.

tasks.task_intent: Analyze and process large datasets with statistical software.
tasks.prompt: Using a large public health dataset (for example, the CDC's behavioral risk factor survey with several hundred thousand respondents), analyze the relationship between hours of sleep and self-reported poor mental health days. Write the analysis report: how you load and subset the data, why and how you apply survey weights and design variables, handling of missing and 'don't know' responses, the model used, results presented with confidence intervals, and limitations. Cite the data source and year.

rubric.description: Uses survey weights and design variables properly for population estimates and standard errors.
Recodes special response codes and handles missing data transparently.
Interprets associations without causal claims and notes self-report and cross-sectional limits.

reference_answer_outline: Load the annual file; subset adults with valid sleep and mental health items.
Recode codes for don't know and refused to missing; define sleep categories.
Survey-weighted estimates with strata and cluster variables.
Model: survey-weighted regression with age, sex and other controls.
Limitations: cross-sectional, self-reported, possible reverse causation.

tasks.task_intent: Design and review insurance, annuity and pension products, checking that they are financially sound and setting premiums.
tasks.prompt: A startup wants to sell one-year accident-and-illness pet insurance for dogs with a 250 deductible and 80 percent reimbursement up to 5,000. Using clearly invented claim data (claim frequency and average claim by age band), compute a pure premium per age band, add expense and profit loads to get a gross premium, test sensitivity to a 20 percent rise in claim frequency, and write a memo on whether the plan is financially sound, what data you would need before launch, and what regulatory review applies.

rubric.description: Pure premium equals frequency times severity after deductible and coinsurance; loads are applied correctly.
Sensitivity analysis is computed and its effect on soundness explained, including adverse selection.
Memo identifies data gaps and that rates and forms need regulatory filing and actuarial sign-off.

reference_answer_outline: Expected paid claim: frequency times (severity minus deductible) times 0.8, capped.
Gross premium equals pure premium divided by (1 minus expense and profit ratio).
Sensitivity: 20 percent frequency increase raises the loss ratio by about the same proportion.
Risks: older dogs, breed effects, anti-selection, small data.
Need credible claims data or reinsurance; state filing and qualified actuary review.

tasks.task_intent: Give technical help for existing reports, dashboards and other analysis tools.
tasks.prompt: Invented ticket: the sales director says the regional revenue dashboard shows 4.2 million for last month while the finance report shows 4.6 million, and she presents to the board tomorrow. Write how you would handle the ticket: the first response to the director, a step-by-step diagnosis (filters, refresh status, definitions such as booked versus invoiced revenue, time zones, currency, returns), how you document the root cause and fix, and how you prevent this kind of mismatch in the future.

rubric.description: Acknowledges urgency, sets expectations and gives a timeline.
Checks likely causes in a sensible order and reconciles the two numbers to the source.
Documents root cause and adds definitions, reconciliation checks or data alerts.

reference_answer_outline: Reply within the hour with a plan and time of next update.
Check refresh timestamp, filters, date ranges, revenue definition, returns and currency conversion.
Reconcile both figures to the general ledger; identify the gap's components.
Fix dashboard logic or add a note; tell the director which number to use for the board and why.
Prevention: shared metric definitions, automated daily reconciliation, data freshness label.

tasks.task_intent: Recommend data-based solutions to key stakeholders.
tasks.prompt: Invented results: an online bookstore ran a three-week A/B test of free shipping over 25 versus over 35. Conversion rose from 3.1 to 3.4 percent (about 120,000 visitors per arm), average order value fell from 41 to 37, and shipping costs per order rose by 0.80. Write a one-page recommendation to the executive team: statistical significance and confidence intervals, the profit impact per 1,000 visitors under stated margin assumptions, risks such as novelty effects, and your recommendation with a follow-up plan.

rubric.description: Tests the conversion difference and reports uncertainty correctly for the stated sample sizes.
Converts results into profit per visitor with explicit margin assumptions.
Makes a decision-oriented recommendation that weighs uncertainty and proposes follow-up.

reference_answer_outline: Difference 0.3 points; standard error from both proportions; significant at the stated sample size.
Revenue per 1,000 visitors: 34 orders times 37 versus 31 orders times 41.
Profit using a margin assumption minus extra shipping cost.
Risks: novelty, seasonality, effects on repeat purchases.
Recommendation depends on profit result; follow-up test of threshold 30.

tasks.task_intent: Estimate rates of death, accidents, illness, disability and retirement from statistical data.
tasks.prompt: Invented data: a pension plan observed 2,000 members aged 60 to 64 for three years with total exposure of 5,700 person-years and 34 deaths, and 1,500 members aged 65 to 69 with 4,200 person-years and 52 deaths. Estimate the central death rate for each age band with a confidence interval, compare them with a published national life table (cite which one you would use) via actual-to-expected ratios, explain whether the plan's data are credible enough to use alone, and recommend how to blend plan experience with the standard table.

rubric.description: Computes rates as deaths over exposure and gives a sensible interval (e.g. Poisson-based).
Calculates actual-to-expected ratios against a cited standard table correctly.
Discusses credibility given the small number of deaths and recommends a reasoned blending approach.

reference_answer_outline: Rates about 0.0060 and 0.0124 per person-year.
Poisson interval: deaths plus or minus about 1.96 times the square root of deaths, divided by exposure.
Expected deaths from the table's rates times exposure; actual-to-expected ratios.
Limited credibility with under 100 deaths per band.
Blend with credibility weighting or apply a scaling factor to the standard table.

tasks.format: data delivery schedule and service levels
tasks.task_intent: Make sure business-intelligence information reaches its users on time.
tasks.prompt: A regional grocery chain's BI team delivers nightly sales dashboards, a weekly inventory report and monthly finance extracts to 300 users, and data have arrived late four times this month. Write a plan to manage the flow: map the data pipeline steps and dependencies, set delivery times and service levels for each product, define monitoring and alerting for late or failed loads, a communication process when data are late, and a monthly review of reliability metrics.

rubric.description: Maps sources, transformations and dependencies and identifies likely bottlenecks.
Each product has a delivery time, freshness indicator and owner.
Includes automated alerts, status notices to users and reliability metrics with review.

reference_answer_outline: Pipeline: point-of-sale export, warehouse load, transformations, dashboard refresh.
Service levels: dashboards by 6:00, inventory Monday 8:00, finance on business day 2.
Alerts if a job fails or runs late; on-call rotation.
User status banner and email when data are late, with estimated time.
Monthly on-time rate, incidents and root causes reviewed with stakeholders.

tasks.task_intent: Determine what a substance is made of and how it behaves, using instrumental techniques such as chromatography and spectroscopy.
tasks.prompt: A consumer group asks your lab whether five energy drinks contain the caffeine amounts on their labels and whether any contain an undeclared stimulant. Write the analytical plan: sample preparation (degassing, dilution, filtration), the technique for quantifying caffeine (for example, HPLC with UV detection) and how you build the calibration curve, how you would screen for other stimulants (such as LC-MS), quality controls (blanks, duplicates, spiked recovery), how you calculate and report results with uncertainty, and how you decide whether a label is inaccurate.

rubric.description: Chooses suitable separation and detection methods and justifies them for caffeine and for screening unknowns.
Includes calibration with standards, blanks, duplicates, spike recovery and acceptance criteria.
Calculates concentration per serving with uncertainty and sets a clear rule for judging label accuracy.

reference_answer_outline: Degas, dilute into the calibration range, filter through a 0.45 micrometer filter.
Reversed-phase HPLC with UV near 273 nm; five-point calibration; check linearity.
Screening for undeclared stimulants by LC-MS against reference standards.
QC: method blank, duplicate injections, spike recovery between about 90 and 110 percent.
Report milligrams per serving with expanded uncertainty; flag labels outside a stated tolerance.

tasks.task_intent: Set and consistently apply rules and routines that keep a classroom orderly.
tasks.prompt: You are a new high school chemistry teacher; your first wet lab (reactions of acids with metals and carbonates) is in week three. Write the rules and routines plan: the lab-safety rules you will teach and how students show they understand them before any lab, routines for goggles, chemical pickup and waste disposal, how you signal stop, what happens if a student breaks a safety rule versus a general classroom rule, and how routines are taught in the first weeks.

rubric.description: Rules address eye protection, chemical handling, waste, spills, and no food or drink, matched to the planned lab.
Routines are modeled and rehearsed, with a safety quiz or contract before the first lab.
Distinguishes immediate removal for safety violations from graduated responses for other misbehavior and applies them consistently.

reference_answer_outline: Rules: goggles on from start to cleanup, read labels twice, never return chemicals to stock bottles, report spills and injuries immediately.
Routines: materials table pickup by one student per group, labeled waste containers, stop signal.
Safety quiz with a minimum score required before lab participation.
Safety violation: removal from the lab activity with an alternative task and family contact.
Rehearse a mock spill drill in week one.

tasks.task_intent: Get ready for, or take part in, quality audits by study sponsors, government agencies or special review groups.
tasks.prompt: Your clinical research site has been told a sponsor will audit a diabetes drug study in four weeks, and that a regulatory inspection could follow. Write the audit-readiness plan: the documents to review (regulatory binder, consent forms, delegation log, training records, investigational product accountability, source documents versus case report forms), a sampling approach for self-checking participant records, how findings are corrected without backdating, staff preparation, and the logistics for the audit days.

rubric.description: Covers essential documents, consent, eligibility, product accountability, adverse event reporting and data consistency.
Corrections follow good documentation practice (dated, initialed, explained); no backdating or recreating records.
Staff know their roles and the audit days are planned (workspace, access, contact person, daily debrief).

reference_answer_outline: Checklist of essential documents and current versions.
Review all consents and a sample of participant files for eligibility and source-to-database agreement.
Product accountability: dispensing logs reconcile with returns and stock.
Corrections documented with date, initials and reason; notes to file where needed.
Audit logistics: room, monitor access to records, coordinator available, daily wrap-up.

tasks.task_intent: Work with scientists and engineers to study a project's chemistry, make sense of test data, or devise special-purpose tests.
tasks.prompt: Invented case: a process engineer reports that the last three batches of a polyurethane coating cure tacky, although every standard QC test passed. You meet the engineer and the formulation chemist. Write the meeting summary and plan: the questions you asked, hypotheses (moisture in raw materials, catalyst level, isocyanate-to-polyol ratio, cure temperature), the existing data you reviewed, a non-standard test you propose (for example, FTIR monitoring of isocyanate peak during cure or Karl Fischer water testing of raw materials), and how results will decide the fix.

rubric.description: Captures input from both colleagues and asks questions that separate hypotheses.
Hypotheses are chemically plausible and the proposed tests can confirm or rule them out.
States what result points to which corrective action and how quickly it can be tested.

reference_answer_outline: Questions: raw material lots, humidity during mixing, mixing ratios, cure oven logs.
Hypotheses ranked by likelihood with evidence for each.
Tests: Karl Fischer on polyol lots, FTIR of residual isocyanate over time, small batches at controlled ratios.
Decision tree: high water means drying or new supplier lot; off-ratio means meter calibration.
Owners and dates; summary shared with QC and production.

tasks.task_intent: Adjust teaching approaches and materials to suit students' different needs and interests.
tasks.prompt: Your 10th-grade chemistry class is starting stoichiometry. A pre-test shows some students are unsure about ratios and unit conversions, most are ready, and a few have already learned mole calculations. Plan a 55-minute lesson with differentiation: the shared goal, a hands-on hook (for example, a recipe-scaling activity), tiered practice sets, scaffolds such as worked examples and unit-tracking organizers, an extension involving limiting reactants, and a common exit ticket.

rubric.description: Mole ratios and conversions are correct and the hook maps clearly to chemical equations.
Tiers vary support and challenge while targeting the same goal.
Exit ticket measures the shared goal and informs grouping for the next lesson.

reference_answer_outline: Goal: use a balanced equation to convert moles of one substance to another.
Hook: scale a sandwich recipe, then link to reactant ratios.
Tier 1: worked examples with unit organizer; Tier 2: standard problems; Tier 3: limiting reactant puzzles.
Teacher checks in with each group; peer explainers.
Exit ticket: one mole-to-mole and one mass-to-mass problem.

tasks.task_intent: Keep track of participants' enrollment status and record why participants drop out and what was done to reach them.
tasks.prompt: A 12-month nutrition study at your site aims to enroll 150 participants and has lost 11 of the first 60. Design the tracking system: the fields in the enrollment and retention log (screening, consent, randomization, visit dates, status, withdrawal reason categories, contact attempts), how contact attempts are documented, weekly reports to the investigator, how you protect participant privacy in the log, and two retention strategies suggested by the dropout reasons you invent and label.

rubric.description: Fields capture each stage and use standardized withdrawal reason categories and contact-attempt records.
Weekly report shows enrollment versus target, retention rate and trends in dropout reasons.
Log uses participant IDs rather than names where possible, and retention strategies follow from the reasons.

reference_answer_outline: Fields: participant ID, screen date, consent version, randomization arm, visit windows, status, withdrawal reason code, last contact.
Contact attempts: date, method, outcome; protocol-defined lost-to-follow-up rule.
Report: cumulative enrollment chart, retention percent, reasons table.
Identifiers kept in a separate restricted file.
Retention ideas: flexible visit times, transport support, reminder texts.

tasks.task_intent: Set and consistently apply rules and routines that keep a classroom orderly.
tasks.prompt: You teach high school physics with frequent hands-on labs (carts on ramps, projectile launchers, springs, a low-power laser). Write the classroom rules and routines plan: expectations stated positively, routines for lab groups, equipment checkout and return, a clear stop signal, what happens when a rule is broken during a launch activity, and how you will teach and practice these routines during the first two weeks.

rubric.description: Rules address launch zones, eye protection, laser safety and equipment handling.
Group roles, checkout and return procedures and signals are concrete.
Responses are graduated for general behavior and immediate for safety risks, and routines are rehearsed.

reference_answer_outline: Expectations: respect launch zones, goggles for projectiles and springs, never look into or point the laser at anyone.
Group roles: materials manager, recorder, safety checker.
Checkout sheet; equipment returned and counted before dismissal.
Stop signal: lights off or a bell; hands off equipment.
Safety violation leads to removal from the launch station with an alternative data-analysis task.

tasks.task_intent: Supervise crews that withdraw water from groundwater wells and rivers.
tasks.prompt: You are the water resource specialist supervising a three-person field crew running a 72-hour pumping test on a new municipal well and taking river-flow measurements nearby to see if pumping affects the river. Write the supervision plan: crew roles and shift schedule, equipment and calibration checks (pressure transducers, flow meter), the measurement schedule, safety (traffic, river wading, electrical generator), data recording and handoffs between shifts, and how you decide to stop or extend the test.

rubric.description: Roles, shifts and handoffs cover 72 hours without gaps or fatigue risks.
Instruments are calibrated and the schedule captures rapid early drawdown and recovery.
Covers field hazards with controls and defines stop or extend criteria.

reference_answer_outline: Three 8-hour shifts with overlap for handoff; supervisor on call.
Transducers in pumping and observation wells, calibrated beforehand; manual checks with a water-level meter.
Log-spaced readings early, then hourly; recovery monitoring after shutdown.
Safety: traffic cones, PFDs and no wading at high flow, generator grounding.
Stop if discharge cannot be held constant or drawdown nears the pump intake.

tasks.task_intent: Teach students to use equipment and materials properly and supervise them so no one is hurt and nothing is damaged.
tasks.prompt: Before a unit on electric circuits, your physics students will use DC power supplies, breadboards, multimeters and small resistors that can get hot. Plan the instruction and supervision: a short demonstration of correct use, the common mistakes that cause injury or damage (short circuits, wrong meter setting), a 'license' check each student passes before independent use, how you position yourself and monitor during lab time, and what to do if a component overheats.

rubric.description: Explains correct use of power supplies and meters (current limit, measuring current in series, voltage in parallel).
Students show competence in a check before independent use.
Describes monitoring strategies and a clear response to overheating or smoke.

reference_answer_outline: Demo: set current limit low, build circuit with power off, check before switching on.
Mistakes: meter on current setting across a source, shorted leads, touching hot resistors.
License check: build a simple circuit and measure voltage and current correctly.
Teacher circulates with a scan pattern; groups raise a card for a circuit check.
Overheating: switch off at the supply, do not touch, let cool, report.

tasks.task_intent: Teach a subject through explanation, discussion and demonstration.
tasks.prompt: Plan a 50-minute physics lesson on Newton's second law. Include a demonstration (for example, a cart pulled by a hanging mass with a motion sensor or phone accelerometer), a short explanation that connects net force, mass and acceleration, a discussion that confronts the common belief that motion requires a continuing force, and a quick formative check. Explain how students use the demonstration's data in the explanation.

rubric.description: Correctly relates net force, mass and acceleration and addresses the force-implies-motion misconception.
The demonstration produces data (acceleration for different masses) that students analyze.
Includes a meaningful check, such as predicting acceleration for a new mass, and adapts based on results.

reference_answer_outline: Prediction prompt before the demo.
Demo: vary hanging mass and cart mass; record acceleration.
Plot acceleration against net force for constant mass; slope relates to mass.
Discussion: a hockey puck on ice keeps moving without a push.
Check: two quick prediction problems with mini whiteboards.

tasks.task_intent: Bargain with towns or water utilities over water rights so that supply covers demand.
tasks.prompt: Invented case: in a drought year, your regional water authority needs an extra 2 million cubic meters over the summer, and a neighboring irrigation district holds senior rights to the river. Prepare a negotiation brief: each side's interests and constraints, your best alternative if no deal is reached, options for a deal (temporary lease, fallowing payments, exchange of treated wastewater, dry-year option contracts), how you would value the water, legal or regulatory approvals required, and how you will communicate with affected farmers and residents.

rubric.description: Identifies interests of both sides, not just positions, and a realistic alternative to agreement.
Proposes several deal structures with a reasoned price range.
Notes required approvals under water law and plans fair, transparent communication.

reference_answer_outline: Authority interests: reliable summer supply, cost; district interests: crop income, long-term rights, community.
Alternative: emergency conservation and groundwater pumping.
Options: one-year lease, payments for fallowing specific fields, recycled water exchange, multi-year dry-year option.
Value using farm net income lost plus a premium; compare with alternative supply cost.
Approvals from the state water agency; public meetings and written FAQs.

tasks.task_intent: Model the hydrology, hydraulics or water quality of a system.
tasks.prompt: A town wants to know whether a grassy drainage channel can carry the peak runoff from a new 12-hectare housing development. Using stated, labeled assumptions, estimate the peak flow with the rational method (runoff coefficient, rainfall intensity for the design storm, area), then use Manning's equation to check whether a trapezoidal channel with given dimensions and slope can carry it. Show all calculations, discuss the sensitivity of the answer to the runoff coefficient and roughness, and state when a more detailed model would be needed.

rubric.description: Rational method and Manning's equation are applied with consistent units and correct geometry.
Shows how the result changes with plausible ranges of runoff coefficient and roughness.
Explains when a hydrograph or computer model (such as for larger areas or storage) is required.

reference_answer_outline: Peak flow equals C times i times A with unit conversion; e.g. C around 0.5 for suburban lots.
Channel area and hydraulic radius for the trapezoid; Manning flow with n around 0.03 to 0.04 for grass.
Compare capacity with peak flow; freeboard.
Sensitivity table for C and n.
Rational method is limited to small catchments; use hydrograph modeling for detention design.

tasks.task_intent: Build, clean, transform and look after large research datasets.
tasks.prompt: A psychology lab ran an online survey on sleep and stress with 2,400 student responses exported from the survey platform: wide format, item names like Q14_3, some reverse-scored items, attention-check questions, and a free-text 'major' field. Write a data management plan for turning this into an analysis-ready dataset: a codebook template, the cleaning steps in order (including attention-check exclusions and reverse scoring), how you compute scale scores, how you keep the raw file untouched and record every change, and how identifying information is protected.

rubric.description: Raw data stays read-only and all transformations are scripted or logged so another person could rebuild the dataset.
Reverse-scoring, scale scoring and handling of missing items are described correctly, and exclusion rules are stated before looking at outcomes.
Identifiers are separated or removed, storage and access are controlled, and the plan follows the study's consent and ethics approval.

reference_answer_outline: Codebook: variable name, label, item wording reference, response scale, reverse-scored flag, missing codes.
Order: import, rename, flag failed attention checks, recode reverse items, compute scales, recode free-text majors into categories.
Scale scores as mean of items with a stated minimum number answered.
Raw export kept read-only; analysis script under version control; change log.
Remove emails and IP addresses into a separate locked file; access limited to approved staff.

tasks.task_intent: Carry out neuropsychological evaluations covering abilities such as intelligence, attention, language, learning and memory.
tasks.prompt: Graduate-path practice: neuropsychological testing is administered and interpreted by licensed psychologists or trained psychometrists under supervision. Imagine you are a research assistant helping a supervising neuropsychologist plan a four-hour outpatient evaluation for a 66-year-old retired teacher whose family reports forgetfulness. Draft the session plan: the cognitive domains to cover and why, examples of the kinds of standardized measures used for each domain, the order of testing and breaks, how fatigue, hearing or vision problems and language background affect validity, and what information you would collect before the visit.

rubric.description: Covers the relevant domains (memory, attention, processing speed, language, visuospatial, executive function, mood screening) and justifies each for a memory complaint.
Addresses performance validity, sensory limits, fatigue, education and language effects on norms.
Correctly keeps administration and interpretation with qualified staff and includes consent and confidentiality.

reference_answer_outline: Pre-visit: referral question, medical history, medications, education, primary language, collateral report from family.
Domains with example measure types, such as list-learning memory tests and timed attention tasks, plus a depression screen.
Order: harder memory tasks early with delayed recall intervals planned; breaks every hour.
Check hearing aids and glasses; choose norms appropriate to age and education; include validity indicators.
Assistant's role limited to scheduling, setup and supervised tasks; results reported by the neuropsychologist.

tasks.task_intent: Compare how patients are doing before and after a medication, surgery or behavioral treatment.
tasks.prompt: Invented data: a clinic tested 12 patients with epilepsy on a verbal memory test before and six months after surgery. Scores (standard scores, mean 100, SD 15): before 92, 88, 101, 85, 97, 90, 105, 83, 94, 99, 87, 91; after 86, 90, 95, 78, 98, 85, 100, 84, 89, 97, 80, 92. The test's test-retest reliability is 0.85. Write a one-page analysis: the group-level change, a reliable change index for individuals, how many patients show reliable decline, what practice effects and regression to the mean mean for interpretation, and how you would present the findings to the surgical team.

rubric.description: Computes mean change and a reliable change index correctly from the stated reliability and SD, showing the formula.
Discusses practice effects, regression to the mean, small sample size and the lack of a control group.
Presents results clearly to clinicians, separating group trends from individual cases and stating limits.

reference_answer_outline: Mean before about 92.7, after about 89.5; change about minus 3 points.
Standard error of difference from SD times the square root of 2 times (1 minus reliability); about 8.2, so the RCI threshold is roughly 16 points at 95 percent.
Few or no patients pass the strict threshold; some show declines of 5 to 7 points worth monitoring.
Practice effects could hide true decline; repeat testing would ideally use practice-adjusted RCI and a comparison group.
Report a table per patient and a short summary noting uncertainty.

tasks.task_intent: Check that data entered into research databases are accurate and valid, and fix the errors found.
tasks.prompt: Paper questionnaires from 300 participants in a parenting-stress study were typed into a database by four student assistants. Design and run (on paper) a verification audit: how you will select records for double entry, the range and logic checks you will script (for example, a child's age older than the parent's, a 1 to 5 item coded 6), how you will decide what is a correctable error versus missing data, how every correction is recorded, and the error-rate threshold that would trigger re-entering a whole batch.

rubric.description: Uses a defensible sample (random or full double entry for key fields) and lists specific range, consistency and duplicate checks.
Corrections are made only against the source document, with clear rules for unresolvable values.
Every change is logged (who, when, old and new value), and an explicit error-rate threshold triggers re-entry or retraining.

reference_answer_outline: Double-enter a random 10 to 20 percent of forms plus all primary outcome items.
Scripted checks: out-of-range codes, impossible combinations, duplicate participant IDs, skipped pages.
Look up each flagged value on the paper form; if illegible, code as missing with a reason code.
Change log stored with the dataset; original entries preserved.
If a batch error rate exceeds about 1 percent of fields, re-enter that batch and retrain that assistant.

tasks.task_intent: Discuss patients' neurological conditions with other professionals.
tasks.prompt: Graduate-path practice. Invented case: a 16-year-old athlete had a concussion five weeks ago and still reports headaches and trouble concentrating; testing by the supervising neuropsychologist found slowed processing speed but normal memory. Draft the consultation materials the neuropsychologist could use: (1) a short consult note to the treating neurologist, and (2) talking points for a meeting with the school counselor about temporary academic accommodations. Keep medical decisions with the physician and share only information the family has authorized.

rubric.description: The note to the neurologist is concise and technical; the school talking points are plain-language and focus on function and accommodations.
Does not make medical decisions such as clearance to play; defers return-to-sport to the physician and follows concussion protocols.
Shares only what the family has authorized and avoids unnecessary diagnostic detail with the school.

reference_answer_outline: Neurologist note: referral question, key findings (processing speed below expectation, memory within normal limits), impressions, recommendation to re-evaluate in a set number of weeks.
School points: extra time on tests, rest breaks, reduced screen load, gradual return to full workload.
Defer return-to-play to the physician's graduated protocol.
Confirm signed release of information before school contact.
Plan follow-up contact to review whether accommodations can be reduced.

tasks.task_intent: Design or deliver plans that help people recover or work around impaired thinking skills.
tasks.prompt: Graduate-path practice. Invented case: a 52-year-old office manager had a stroke four months ago and has trouble remembering appointments, tracking multi-step tasks and staying focused in a noisy office. She wants to return to work part-time in two months. Draft a cognitive rehabilitation plan the supervising clinician could review: goals written in measurable terms, compensatory strategies and tools, any restorative practice, how the employer and family are involved, and how progress is measured every two weeks.

rubric.description: Goals are specific and functional, e.g. uses a calendar system to keep a stated share of appointments without reminders.
Prioritizes compensatory strategies (external memory aids, checklists, environmental changes) and explains any restorative exercises realistically.
Tracks progress with defined measures and includes the patient, family and employer in planning with consent.

reference_answer_outline: Goals for calendar use, completing multi-step tasks with checklists, and sustained work in 30-minute blocks.
Tools: smartphone calendar with alarms, written task templates, noise-reducing headphones, quieter workstation.
Strategy training using goal-setting and self-monitoring routines; practice with real work tasks.
Workplace plan with graded hours and agreed accommodations.
Biweekly review of goal attainment and a brief rating scale; adjust plan.

tasks.task_intent: Conduct, receive or check the regular counts of incarcerated people.
tasks.prompt: Practice for a later supervisory role (supervisor roles normally require prior line experience). You supervise the evening shift in a 400-bed county jail. Write the procedure for a scheduled formal count: how officers count, how counts are reported and reconciled with the population record, the time limits, what happens if the count does not clear (recount, lockdown, notifications), and how the count and any discrepancy are documented.

rubric.description: Count method ensures each person is physically observed and reconciled with records.
Clear escalation for a count that does not clear, including recount and notifications.
Records times, officers, numbers, discrepancies and resolution.

reference_answer_outline: All movement stops; officers count by sight, verifying living, breathing persons.
Housing units report to central control; reconcile with roster including court, medical and work assignments.
Recount within set minutes; if still off, lockdown and name check.
Notify the shift commander and follow escape or emergency procedures.
Count sheets signed and retained.

tasks.task_intent: Explain police operations and procedures to subordinate officers so they can do their jobs.
tasks.prompt: Practice for a later supervisory role. Your department adopted an updated body-worn camera policy: cameras must be activated at the start of every enforcement contact, officers may not review footage before writing a use-of-force report until after an initial statement, and certain sensitive locations require notification. Prepare a 10-minute roll-call briefing: key changes, why they matter, three realistic scenarios to discuss, likely questions with answers, and how you will check that officers understand and follow the policy.

rubric.description: States changes accurately and explains reasons such as transparency and evidence integrity.
Scenarios are realistic and promote discussion of judgment calls.
Includes follow-up such as footage audits and coaching.

reference_answer_outline: What changed and effective date.
Reasons: public trust, evidence quality, legal requirements.
Scenarios: traffic stop that escalates, medical call, interview in a hospital.
Answers to questions on privacy and malfunctions.
Monthly random footage audits and individual feedback.

tasks.task_intent: Supervise and direct correctional officers so incarcerated people are kept safely, with discipline and care for their welfare.
tasks.prompt: Practice for a later supervisory role. You supervise 12 officers on a night shift with two officers out sick, a housing unit with recent fights, and a medical transport scheduled at 03:00. Write the shift plan: post assignments and minimum staffing, briefing priorities, how you supervise rounds and security checks, response plans for a fight or medical emergency, and how you ensure humane treatment and documentation throughout the shift.

rubric.description: Assigns posts to cover critical areas and handles shortages within policy.
Defines checks on rounds, communication and incident response.
Includes humane treatment, medical access and full documentation.

reference_answer_outline: Post chart; overtime or reassignments to cover minimums.
Briefing: tension in the unit, transport details, officer safety.
Supervisor tours and verification of round logs.
Emergency response roles; medical escort procedures.
Shift log entries and incident reports before end of shift.

tasks.task_intent: Look into and resolve personnel problems and complaints of misconduct against staff.
tasks.prompt: Practice for a later supervisory role. A resident files a complaint that an officer was rude and refused to give his badge number during a traffic stop; footage exists. Write the investigation plan: intake and classification of the complaint, notice to the officer and rights under policy and any labor agreement, evidence to gather (footage, dispatch records, witness statements), interview approach, the standard of proof and possible findings, and how the complainant is informed of the outcome.

rubric.description: Follows policy and due-process protections for the officer and treats the complainant respectfully.
Collects and weighs objective evidence before interviews and conclusions.
Uses defined findings categories and communicates the outcome appropriately.

reference_answer_outline: Log and classify as a courtesy complaint; assign investigator.
Notify officer per contract; preserve footage.
Gather footage, CAD records, witness information.
Interviews: complainant first, then officer; record statements.
Findings: sustained, not sustained, exonerated, unfounded; letter to complainant.

tasks.task_intent: Watch how officers behave to make sure they are alert, courteous and professional with incarcerated people, coworkers, visitors and the public.
tasks.prompt: Practice for a later supervisory role. After visitor complaints about disrespectful treatment at a jail's visiting area, you are asked to improve officers' professional conduct. Write the monitoring and feedback plan: observable behaviors you will look for, how you observe (walkthroughs, camera review, visitor feedback), how you give feedback and coaching, recognition for good conduct, and when you escalate to formal discipline.

rubric.description: Professional conduct is described in observable terms.
Uses direct observation, video and feedback sources fairly.
Balances coaching and recognition with consistent escalation.

reference_answer_outline: Behaviors: greeting, clear explanations of rules, calm tone, no sarcasm.
Weekly walkthroughs, random video review, visitor comment cards.
Same-day private feedback; coaching plans.
Recognition in briefings and evaluations.
Repeated or serious incidents referred under the discipline policy.

tasks.task_intent: Keep logs, write reports and direct how departmental records are produced, handled and stored.
tasks.prompt: Practice for a later supervisory role. Your squad's incident reports are often late or incomplete, and a recent court case was harmed by a missing evidence log entry. Write a records plan for your squad: report quality standards, review and approval timelines, evidence and chain-of-custody logging, storage and retention requirements, public records requests, and how you train officers and track compliance.

rubric.description: Defines what complete, accurate reports must include.
Addresses evidence logging, secure storage and retention rules.
Includes training and measurable tracking such as on-time report rate.

reference_answer_outline: Report standards: who, what, when, where, how, narrative clarity.
Supervisor review within one shift; returned reports corrected within 24 hours.
Evidence logged at intake with continuous custody records.
Retention schedule; public records requests routed to records unit.
Weekly metrics and refresher training.

tasks.task_intent: Interview clients alone, with family members or in groups to understand their circumstances, strengths and difficulties and decide which services they need.
tasks.prompt: Invented case: a school refers a family because a 9-year-old has missed 22 days this semester; the mother works night shifts and the family recently moved in with relatives. Write the intake interview guide for a home visit: how you open and explain your role and confidentiality limits, strengths-based and open questions for the parent and age-appropriate questions for the child, how you assess safety, the information you need to decide on services, cultural humility considerations, and how you close and agree on next steps.

rubric.description: Explains role, consent and mandated-reporting limits clearly and builds rapport respectfully.
Questions cover needs, strengths, supports, housing, work schedules, health and child safety.
Links information gathered to specific service options and agreed next steps.

reference_answer_outline: Introduction: who you are, why the referral, what is confidential and what is not.
Parent questions: daily routine, barriers to attendance, supports, what has worked before.
Child questions in simple language about school and home.
Safety screening per agency tools.
Next steps: transport assistance, school liaison, childcare, follow-up date.

tasks.task_intent: Assemble and keep up a case file for each assigned offender.
tasks.prompt: You have been assigned a caseload of 60 people on probation. Design the case file structure and maintenance routine: the sections every file must have (court orders and conditions, risk and needs assessment, supervision plan, contacts, drug test results, treatment reports, violations, correspondence), naming and dating conventions, what must be updated after each contact and within what time, privacy and record-access rules, and a monthly self-audit checklist.

rubric.description: File sections cover legal, assessment, plan, contact and compliance records.
Sets clear update deadlines and contact note standards.
Addresses access rules for sensitive records (such as treatment information) and includes a self-audit.

reference_answer_outline: Sections in a standard order, electronic or paper.
Contact notes within 24 hours; objective and specific.
Treatment records handled under substance-use confidentiality rules.
Access limited to authorized staff; release requires proper consent.
Monthly check: conditions tracked, assessments current, deadlines met.

tasks.task_intent: Track, assess and record how clients are moving toward their treatment goals.
tasks.prompt: Graduate-path practice (clinical social work is typically a master's-level, licensed role). Invented case: a 34-year-old client in outpatient treatment for alcohol use and depression has goals of reducing drinking days and returning to work. Design the progress-monitoring plan: measurable indicators for each goal, standardized measures you would use and how often, how the client participates in reviewing data, how you write progress notes, and what changes in the data would lead you to adjust the plan with the supervisor.

rubric.description: Each goal has observable, measurable indicators and a baseline.
Uses suitable validated tools at sensible intervals.
Client reviews progress with the worker, and clear criteria trigger plan changes.

reference_answer_outline: Indicators: drinking days per week, depression score, job search activities.
Measures: a depression questionnaire every two weeks, timeline follow-back for drinking.
Shared graph reviewed in sessions.
Progress notes in a structured format such as DAP or SOAP.
No improvement after about six weeks leads to case review and possible referral.

tasks.task_intent: Create and revisit service plans together with clients and follow up to check how much and how well services were delivered.
tasks.prompt: Continuing the school-attendance case, write a 90-day service plan developed with the mother: two or three family-chosen goals written in measurable terms, the services and who provides them, the family's own action steps, how and when you follow up to check whether services actually happened and helped, and how the plan will be revised. Write it in plain language the family can keep.

rubric.description: Goals reflect the family's priorities and are measurable and time-bound.
Each goal has named services, providers and family steps.
Plans checks on whether services were delivered and helpful, with revision points.

reference_answer_outline: Goals: child attends at least 90 percent of days; stable morning routine; housing application submitted.
Services: school transport, after-school program, housing navigator.
Family steps: alarm routine, contact school when absent.
Follow-up: biweekly calls, monthly home visit, attendance data from school.
Review at 45 and 90 days; revise or close.

tasks.task_intent: Collect background information on offenders by talking with them, their families, friends and others who know relevant facts.
tasks.prompt: A judge orders a presentence investigation for a 23-year-old convicted of a first-time felony theft. Write the information-gathering plan: whom you will interview (the person, family, employer, victim), the records you will request (criminal history, school, employment, treatment), how you verify claims and handle conflicting accounts, how you protect sensitive information, and the structure of the report to the court.

rubric.description: Includes interviews and records relevant to risk, needs and circumstances, including the victim's perspective.
Verifies self-reported information and notes unresolved conflicts.
Respects confidentiality and produces a balanced report format for the court.

reference_answer_outline: Interviews: defendant, family, employer with consent, victim impact.
Records: criminal history, school, employment, treatment with releases.
Verify through documents and second sources; note conflicts.
Sensitive information shared only as permitted.
Report: offense, history, personal background, risk assessment, recommendation.

tasks.task_intent: Supervise or direct the staff who work directly with clients.
tasks.prompt: Graduate-path practice: imagine you are a licensed clinical social worker supervising three bachelor's-level case aides at a community mental-health clinic. Write the supervision plan: weekly structure (individual and group), how you review case notes and caseload safety, training priorities, how you support aides after a difficult client crisis, how you evaluate performance, and the ethical limits on what aides may do.

rubric.description: Schedule and content cover case review, skill development and administration.
Addresses secondary trauma, debriefing and caseload risk.
Defines scope-of-practice limits and fair performance evaluation.

reference_answer_outline: Weekly one-hour individual and biweekly group supervision.
Case note audits and high-risk client review.
Training: crisis de-escalation, documentation, cultural responsiveness.
Debrief after crises; employee assistance referral.
Evaluation against job standards; aides do not provide therapy.

tasks.task_intent: Build, clean, transform and look after large research datasets.
tasks.prompt: An economics professor needs a county-by-month panel for 2015 to 2024 combining unemployment rates from the Bureau of Labor Statistics local area statistics, county population from the Census Bureau, and a list of counties that raised local minimum wages (with effective dates). Write the data-build plan: where each file comes from, the merge keys (county FIPS codes and dates) and pitfalls such as changed county definitions, how you handle missing and revised values, the structure of the final panel, and how the build is scripted and documented for replication.

rubric.description: Names real public sources and merges on FIPS codes and time correctly, noting county boundary changes and annual versus monthly frequency.
Handles revisions, missing values and the event-date variable sensibly and transparently.
Build is fully scripted with a codebook and version notes so others can rebuild it.

reference_answer_outline: Download files with retrieval dates; store raw copies unchanged.
Standardize FIPS as five-digit strings; crosswalk changed counties such as recent Connecticut changes.
Interpolate annual population to months or keep annual and merge by year, documented.
Minimum-wage treatment indicator switches on at the effective month.
Script in R or Python, codebook, README and checksums.

tasks.task_intent: Set and consistently apply rules and routines that keep a classroom orderly.
tasks.prompt: You teach high school economics and plan a lively in-class market simulation where students act as buyers and sellers trading cards for play money. Write the routines and rules that keep it productive: how roles and materials are assigned, signals to start and stop trading, how trades are recorded, rules about respectful bargaining and no side deals, what happens if a student disrupts or cheats, and how you debrief so the activity stays focused on learning.

rubric.description: Roles, materials, signals and recording procedures are specific enough for 30 students to follow.
Rules are stated positively, fit a competitive activity, and consequences are proportionate and consistent.
Routines protect time for data collection and debrief that connects to economic concepts.

reference_answer_outline: Assign buyer and seller cards with private values and costs; trade-recording slips.
Start and stop signal, timed rounds, trades reported to a recorder.
Rules: honest reporting, polite bargaining, stay in the trading area.
Consequences: warning, become a recorder for a round, follow-up conversation.
Debrief: plot recorded prices to see convergence toward equilibrium.

tasks.task_intent: Dig into economic and statistical evidence within a specialty such as labor, finance or agriculture.
tasks.prompt: Using public data (for example, state minimum wages and teen employment from government statistics), write a short applied analysis on whether recent minimum-wage increases in a few states coincided with changes in employment of 16 to 19 year olds. State the question, the data and time period, a simple comparison method (difference-in-differences with comparison states, or an event study), the results you found or would expect to check, threats to causal interpretation, and what the analysis cannot conclude. Cite all data sources.

rubric.description: Question is specific and the data sources, variables and period are clearly identified.
Uses a comparison method suited to policy evaluation and explains its key assumption (parallel trends).
Discusses confounders, small samples and the difference between correlation and causation, and ties conclusions to the evidence.

reference_answer_outline: Question: did teen employment fall relative to comparison states after increases?
Data: state minimum wage histories, employment survey estimates for teens, with sources.
Method: difference-in-differences with pre-trend check.
Threats: regional shocks, sampling error in small groups, policy anticipation.
Conclusion stated with uncertainty and links to the published literature.

tasks.task_intent: Help prepare reports, manuscripts and presentations for research projects.
tasks.prompt: The professor's working paper on minimum wages is due to a conference in ten days and asks you to produce the descriptive-statistics table, two figures (an event-study plot and a map), and the slides' data appendix. Write your production plan: the specifications for each table and figure (variables, labels, notes, units), the style conventions you will follow, how every number is generated by code from the final dataset, how you check the figures against the regression output, and what goes in the replication package.

rubric.description: Tables and figures have clear titles, labeled axes and units, source notes and consistent formatting.
Every number comes from code, and there is a cross-check between tables, figures and text.
Package includes data or access instructions, code, a README and versioned outputs.

reference_answer_outline: Table 1: means and standard deviations by treated and comparison counties, before and after.
Figure 1: event-study coefficients with 95 percent confidence intervals; Figure 2: map of treatment timing.
Export tables and figures directly from scripts; no hand-typed numbers.
Cross-check sample sizes and coefficient values in text against output logs.
Replication folder with raw data links, cleaning and analysis scripts, README and software versions.

tasks.task_intent: Teach a subject through explanation, discussion and demonstration.
tasks.prompt: Plan a 50-minute high school lesson on how supply and demand set prices. Include a short explanation with a hand-drawn graph, a classroom demonstration (for example, an auction of a limited item or the trading simulation), a discussion that applies the model to a current real-world price change students care about (such as concert tickets or gasoline), and an exit question. Show how you check understanding during the lesson and how you support students who find graphs difficult.

rubric.description: Correctly distinguishes changes in quantity demanded from shifts in demand and explains equilibrium.
The demonstration generates evidence students use in the discussion and fits the time.
Includes checks for understanding during the lesson and specific scaffolds for graph reading.

reference_answer_outline: Hook: why do concert ticket prices jump when a tour is announced?
Explain curves, equilibrium, and shifts with one example drawn step by step.
Demonstration: auction with limited supply; record bids to build a demand schedule.
Discussion: apply to a current price change; identify which curve shifted.
Exit question and scaffolds such as a labeled graph template and think-pair-share.

tasks.format: student research team supervision plan (graduate-path practice)
tasks.task_intent: Oversee research projects, including projects carried out by students.
tasks.prompt: Graduate-path practice: imagine you are a senior research assistant asked to run a semester-long project with three undergraduate economics students who will code local housing-permit data for a faculty study. Write the supervision plan: the project's goals and milestones, how you train students and check their work quality, weekly meeting structure, how tasks are divided fairly, how you give feedback, and how students get credit and learning from the experience.

rubric.description: Goals and milestones are concrete with deliverables and dates.
Includes training, a coding manual, double-coding samples and agreement checks.
Describes fair workload, regular feedback, mentoring and appropriate credit.

reference_answer_outline: Milestones: training in week 2, pilot coding by week 4, full coding by week 10, write-up by week 14.
Coding manual with examples; 10 percent double-coded; resolve disagreements weekly.
Weekly 45-minute meeting: progress, problems, one skill session.
Feedback: written notes on coding accuracy and a mid-semester check-in.
Credit: acknowledgment in the paper, a short research presentation, recommendation letters.

tasks.task_intent: Set and consistently apply rules and routines that keep a classroom orderly.
tasks.prompt: You teach 11th-grade government and will hold weekly structured discussions on contested policy questions during an election year. Write the classroom norms and procedures plan: how students help set discussion norms, the routines for structured formats (such as structured academic controversy or Socratic seminar), how you keep discussion civil and evidence-based, your own stance on sharing personal political views, what you do when a comment targets a classmate's identity, and how you communicate the approach to families.

rubric.description: Norms are specific behaviors, co-created with students, and tied to evidence-based argument.
Uses structured discussion formats with clear roles, timing and preparation.
Handles harmful comments promptly and fairly, keeps teacher neutrality appropriate to school policy, and informs families.

reference_answer_outline: Norm-setting lesson; norms posted and revisited.
Formats: structured academic controversy pairs, Socratic seminar inner and outer circles.
Evidence rule: claims backed by sources from a vetted reading set.
Response to identity-targeting comments: stop, restate norm, private follow-up, restorative conversation, school policy if repeated.
Family letter explaining purpose, materials and neutrality policy.

tasks.task_intent: Build, clean, transform and look after large research datasets.
tasks.prompt: A political science faculty member is studying party unity in state legislatures and needs a dataset of all recorded floor votes in three state houses over two sessions. Write the data plan: where the vote records come from (state legislature websites or open legislative data projects), the data structure (bills, roll calls, legislators, individual votes), unique identifiers for legislators who change districts or names, how you code abstentions and absences, how you validate the data against official journals, and how you document it.

rubric.description: Uses linked tables or long format with unique IDs for legislators, bills, roll calls and votes.
Defines consistent coding for yes, no, abstain, absent and paired votes and documents edge cases.
Checks a random sample against official journals and reconciles vote totals.

reference_answer_outline: Sources: state legislature journals and an open legislative data service, with retrieval dates.
Tables: legislators (stable ID, party, district by session), roll calls (date, bill, motion), votes (legislator, roll call, vote code).
Name matching across sessions with a manual review list.
Validation: recompute totals per roll call and compare with official totals; sample 5 percent against journals.
Codebook and change log.

tasks.task_intent: Give instruction in the political science discipline.
